Explain the chapter's central causal chain — a weakened centre, a power vacuum, regional powers and invaders, and the Company's opportunity — and show how each link made the next….
Map-work in words: name the chief regional powers of the century with founder, region and one distinguishing fact each — and mark which two of them the Company would fight within….

cards.title: Decline of the Mughal Empire is the chapter's first story and this node's…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: Decline of the Mughal Empire is the chapter's first story and this node's subject — the PROCESS (not a single event) by which the mightiest state of seventeenth-century India, after Aurangzeb's death in 1707, lost its power while keeping its name: the later Mughals reigned in Delhi until far into the nineteenth century, but after 1707 they no longer RULED. THE DECLINE HAD THREE LAYERS. THE FIRST LAYER IS PERSONAL: the emperors who followed Aurangzeb — Bahadur Shah I (1707–1712), Jahandar Shah (1712–1713), Farrukhsiyar (1713–1719), Muhammad Shah (1719–1748), Ahmad Shah (1748–1754), Alamgir II (1754–1759) and Shah Alam II (1759–1806) — were, with few exceptions, weak, short-reigned or pleasure-loving, and every death on the throne invited a WAR OF SUCCESSION that split the nobility and drained the treasury; king-making passed to court factions, of which the SAYYID BROTHERS (Abdullah Khan and Hussain Ali), who raised Farrukhsiyar to the throne and later deposed and killed him, are the textbook example — in one single year (1719) two puppet princes died in quick succession before Muhammad Shah was placed on the throne. THE SECOND LAYER IS INSTITUTIONAL: the mansabdari–jagirdari machinery that paid the empire's officers with revenue-assignments came under strain — more mansabdars than good jagirs, falling jagir incomes, peasants squeezed harder — the nobility split into factions (Iranis, Turanis, Afghans, Hindustanis), the army lost discipline, drill and up-to-date weapons (and never possessed a navy), and Aurangzeb's last twenty-five years of inconclusive Deccan warfare drained the treasury that fed everything else. THE THIRD LAYER IS THE EXTERNAL BLOW: the empire's visible weakness invited invaders — NADIR SHAH of Iran, who defeated Muhammad Shah's army at Karnal and sacked Delhi in 1739, carrying off the Kohinoor and the Peacock Throne and annexing all Mughal territory west of the Indus; and AHMAD SHAH ABDALI of Afghanistan, who invaded roughly eight times between 1747 and 1767, ending with the Third Battle of Panipat (14 January 1761), in which his army broke the Marathas — the one Indian power still capable of propping up, or replacing, the empire. THE RESULT: by 1765 the emperor Shah Alam II was a defeated pensioner living under the Company's protection, granting away the revenues of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, while the successor states that filled the vacuum (Hyderabad, Awadh, Bengal, the Marathas, the Sikhs, Mysore) are the business of the chapter's next nodes. WHAT DECLINE MEANS, PRECISELY: the loss of authority, army, treasury and prestige — the shell of the empire outlived its power by a century and a half.
steps: The takeaway first: the Mughal empire was not killed in one battle — it died of a hundred self-inflicted wounds, and the invasions of Nadir Shah (1739) and Abdali (1747–1761) were the visible symptoms of a sickness…

Supporting argument 1 — the PERSONAL layer: the later Mughals and their succession wars, learned as a dated roster, are the first cause the examiner asks for. Aurangzeb died in 1707 at Ahmednagar in the Deccan, nearly…

Then the slide: Jahandar Shah (1712–1713) lasted barely a year before his nephew Farrukhsiyar, backed by the SAYYID BROTHERS — Abdullah Khan and Hussain Ali, the two great king-makers of the age — defeated him at Agra.
Farrukhsiyar (1713–1719) owed his throne to those brothers and died by them: deposed, blinded and killed in 1719.
In 1719 alone two puppet princes (Rafi-ud-Darajat and Rafi-ud-Daula) were raised and lost within months, before Muhammad Shah (1719–1748) was installed.

Notice what the roster teaches: the emperorship itself had become a FACTIONAL PRIZE — and a state whose highest office is distributed by assassination has, in the strict sense, no centre left to obey.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., placing Muhammad Shah immediately after Bahadur Shah I "because Rangeela ruled the longest and must have come first") reveals the misconception of roster-by-impression — the order 1713–1719 (Farrukhsiyar) before 1719–1748 (Muhammad Shah)…
remember: RECALL: List the later Mughals from 1707 to 1806 in order, with reign dates, and attach one identifying fact to each — then name the one year in which the throne changed hands….
REASONING: Explain the MECHANISM by which each war of succession left the empire permanently weaker — trace the chain from an emperor's death to a hollowed-out centre, using the….
EVALUATE: A textbook claims: "Aurangzeb destroyed his own empire." Weigh the claim in three parts — two facts that support it, two facts that complicate it, and a verdict that….

cards.title: Rise of Regional Powers is the chapter's second story and this node's subject…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: Rise of Regional Powers is the chapter's second story and this node's subject — the process by which provinces of the weakened Mughal empire became, between 1717 and 1724, de facto kingdoms under their own governors and their own dynasties, while still (on paper) owing allegiance to Delhi: the classic trio are HYDERABAD, AWADH and BENGAL, and their founders are three of the era's exam-compulsory names — the NIZAM-UL-MULK (Asaf Jah) at Hyderabad from 1724, SAADAT KHAN at Awadh from 1722, and MURSHID QULI KHAN at Bengal from 1717. THE MECHANISM IS ONE FORMULA RUN THREE TIMES: a governor holds the emperor's OFFICE (subahdar) → he controls the province's REVENUE (the diwani machinery, the land-tax of India's richest provinces) → out of that revenue he pays his OWN ARMY, loyal to him and not to Delhi → and when the centre cannot punish him, the office turns HEREDITARY: sons and sons-in-law succeed, a dynasty is born. CRUCIALLY, none of the three DECLARED independence: coins were struck in the emperor's name, the emperor's name was read in the Friday prayers, and new rulers sought Delhi's titles and honours — the allegiance was REAL in ceremony and EMPTY in obedience; historians call these states "successor states" for exactly this reason: they did not break the empire, they INHERITED it province by province. THE THREE STATES IN PROFILE: HYDERABAD — the whole Deccan, the largest successor state, founded by the imperial wazir who walked out of a faction-ridden court; AWADH — the rich Ganges plain between Delhi and Bengal, founded by Saadat Khan and carried to power by his son-in-law Safdar Jang and grandson-in-arms Shuja-ud-Daula, with Lucknow rising to be one of India's great cultural capitals; BENGAL — the delta, the RICHEST of all, founded by Murshid Quli Khan the model revenue-administrator (capital moved to Murshidabad), passing through sons-in-law (Shuja-ud-Din, then Sarfaraz Khan) to the usurper ALIVARDI KHAN (1740), whose grandson SIRAJ-UD-DAULAH lost Bengal to the Company at Plassey (1757). THE WIDER MAP: the trio are the GOVERNOR-TYPE successor states; alongside them rose states from below — the Maratha confederacy and the Sikhs — and smaller autonomous powers (the Jats of Bharatpur, the Rohillas of Rohilkhand, the Rajput houses), and later the military state of Mysore: these belong to the chapter's next nodes (03_004–03_006), and the Company's exploitation of the resulting disunity to 03_007. WHY THE NODE MATTERS: it answers the chapter's central causal chain at its second link — the vacuum the weak centre left was filled HERE, region by region — and it plants the two facts the Company's story needs: rich, disunited states, each willing to use the Company against its neighbour.
steps: The takeaway first: the successor states were not rebellions but inheritances — three governors, running the empire's richest provinces with their own revenue and their own armies, simply stopped needing Delhi; learn…
Supporting argument 1 — the MECHANISM is the topic's engine, and it runs in four steps on any province the centre cannot punish.

STEP ONE, the OFFICE: after 1707 the emperors needed capable men to govern distant provinces, and gave them the full imperial apparatus — the subahdar's civil authority and, decisively, the diwan's revenue machinery.
STEP TWO, the REVENUE: Bengal, Awadh and the Deccan were among the richest tax-fields on earth; whoever collected their land-tax controlled wealth greater than Delhi's own shrinking collections.

STEP THREE, the ARMY: revenue paid troops; troops collected revenue from defaulters and frightened neighbours; and because the troops' pay came from the governor and not from Delhi, their loyalty ran to the payer.

STEP FOUR, the DYNASTY: when the governor died, the centre — too weak to impose an outsider — confirmed the son or the son-in-law, took a ceremonial gift (nazr), and blessed what it could not prevent; the office turned…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing that "Alivardi Khan was Murshid Quli Khan's eldest son" — the assumption that all successions ran father-to-son) reveals the misconception of the smooth-ladder Bengal — the chain ran through sons-in-law and ended in usurpation at…
remember: RECALL: Build the successor-states table — for Hyderabad, Awadh and Bengal give founder, founding date, and each founder's one distinguishing fact — then trace Bengal's succession….
REASONING: Explain the four-step mechanism by which a Mughal governor became a king — office, revenue, army, dynasty — and then explain why, having gained all real power, none of….
EVALUATE: "The successor nawabs were traitors who feasted on the empire's corpse." Weigh this charge in three parts: what the charge gets right, what it cannot explain, and the….

cards.title: The Rise of the Maratha Power is the century's greatest rising-from-below and…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The Rise of the Maratha Power is the century's greatest rising-from-below and this node's subject — the transformation, between 1707 and 1761, of a people the Mughals had fought for a generation into the strongest power in India: the state built on SHIVAJI's old kingdom (crowned 1674, dead 1680) was REBUILT by his grandson SHAHU (restored to Maharashtra 1707, seated at Satara) and then EXPANDED beyond all proportion by a line of Brahmin chief ministers — the PESHWAS — whose office became the real throne of the Marathas: BALAJI VISHWANATH (Peshwa from 1713), whose 1719 agreement with the Mughal court granted the Marathas the right to collect CHAUTH (a quarter-share) and SARDESHMUKHI (a tenth-share) of revenue in the Mughal Deccan — the fiscal engine of everything after; BAJI RAO I (Peshwa 1720–1740), the century's most audacious cavalry general, whose horsemen took Malwa and Bundelkhand, raided to the walls of Delhi (1737) and beat the Nizam himself near Bhopal (1737); and BALAJI BAJI RAO (Peshwa 1740–1761), under whom the Marathas became the MUGHAL EMPEROR'S PROTECTORS (from 1752) and their banners reached Lahore (1758) — before the whole edifice met its reckoning at the THIRD BATTLE OF PANIPAT (14 January 1761), where Ahmad Shah Abdali's Afghan army destroyed the Maratha host under Sadashivrao Bhau, killed the Peshwa's son Vishwasrao, and broke the confederacy's northern dream — the Peshwa himself dying within months of grief. THE STATE'S FORM: a CONFEDERACY — the Peshwa's court at Pune beside the four great houses, Scindia (Gwalior), Holkar (Indore), Gaekwad (Baroda) and Bhonsle (Nagpur), each with its army and its lands, united in expansion and divided in command — the very fault-line Panipat exposed. THE PLACEMENT IN THE CHAPTER: the trio of 03_003 INHERITED provinces of the empire; the Marathas ROSE FROM BELOW, a new power claiming the old empire's inheritance by sword and by tax-paper; and when Panipat (1761) crippled them, the vacuum they might have filled passed, within a few years, to the English East India Company (Plassey 1757 behind them, Buxar 1764 and the Diwani 1765 ahead — 03_007's story). WHAT THE NODE TEACHES, PRECISELY: how a people's power is built (legitimacy + a fiscal engine + cavalry), how a confederacy wins and loses, and how one battle can redirect a subcontinent's future.
steps: The takeaway first: the Marathas were the eighteenth century's answer to the question "who inherits the Mughals?" — a people risen from below, powered by a tax-grant (chauth and sardeshmukhi, 1719) and the fastest…
Panipat (14 January 1761) killed that answer in one day, and the question's next answer — the East India Company — was already in the field.

Supporting argument 1 — the FOUNDATION: a restored king and a Brahmin minister's tax-paper built the platform everything else stands on. When Aurangzeb died (1707), the Mughal court released SHAHU — Shivaji's grandson…

Shahu's masterstroke was ministerial: he raised BALAJI VISHWANATH — an able administrator who had begun as a revenue agent — to be his PESHWAS (chief minister) in 1713, and sent him to Delhi's faction-ridden court…
Bank the mechanism: chauth was protection-money — pay us and we do not raid you; sardeshmukhi was the overlord's traditional tenth.
Together they made war PROFITABLE WITHOUT WAR and expansion SELF-FINANCING: every province that paid bought peace; every province that refused financed the army that came.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., starting the ladder with Baji Rao I "because he was the famous one" or placing Madhavrao BEFORE Panipat "because restoration must come first") reveals the misconception of the ladder-by-fame — Balaji Vishwanath's 1719 grant is the…
remember: RECALL: List the four great Peshwas of the eighteenth century in order with their years of office, attaching one dated fact to each — and state what happened to the Peshwa's power….
REASONING: Explain how chauth and sardeshmukhi worked — define each, explain the 1719 grant, and show why this tax-paper converted a fighting people into an expanding state more….
EVALUATE: "Shivaji founded Maratha power….

cards.title: The Other Rising Powers of the Century — this node's subject…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The Other Rising Powers of the Century — this node's subject — are the powers that, like 03_004's Marathas, ROSE FROM BELOW the collapsing Mughal Empire rather than inheriting it as provinces (03_003's trio), and the node features the greatest of them: the SIKHS OF THE PUNJAB. THE ARC, IN DATED STEPS: GURU GOBIND SINGH, the tenth Guru (1675–1708), founded the KHALSA at Anandpur in 1699 — a baptised brotherhood of soldier-saints open to every caste, carrying the five emblems and a mission that made "Sikh" mean both faith and discipline; after his sons fell in the Mughal assault (Chamkaur and Sirhind, 1704) and his own death at Nanded (1708), he left no living Guru — the community itself became the authority. BANDA BAHADUR, the ascetic he commissioned (1708), led the first Sikh rising (1709–1716): SAMANA and SIRHIND taken (Battle of Chappar Chiri, 1710 — Wazir Khan, the killer of the Guru's young sons, slain), the first Sikh coin struck, land-titles granted to the peasants who tilled it — and the rising crushed with terrible cruelty, Banda executed at Delhi (1716). DECADES OF PERSECUTION followed — price put on every Sikh's head — yet the community survived in the deserts and hills, and when Nadir Shah (1739) and Abdali (1747–1761) broke the Punjab's government, the Khalsa's warrior-bands — the MISLS (about twelve; sources count eleven to twelve), bound by the SARBAT KHALSA assembly and the GURMATA (collective resolution) and financed by RAKHI protection-payments — occupied the vacuum. RANJIT SINGH, chief of the small SUKERCHAKIA misl (born 1780), seized LAHORE (1799), was proclaimed MAHARAJA OF PUNJAB (1801), took Amritsar (1802), Multan (1818) and KASHMIR (1819), drilled a modern army with European officers, and by the Treaty of Amritsar (1809) fixed the Sutlej as his boundary with the English East India Company — the last great INDEPENDENT Indian kingdom of the era, which outlived its maker (d. 1839) by a decade. THE PARALLEL RISINGS, BRIEFLY: the JATS of the Agra–Delhi belt, whose fortress-state of BHARATPUR reached its height under SURAJ MAL (d. 1763); and the ROHILLAS, Afghan settler-soldiers of Rohilkhand, organised by ALI MUHAMMAD KHAN and raised to imperial prominence by NAJIB-UD-DAULA, Abdali's ally and Delhi's last strong guard. WHAT THE NODE TEACHES: how persecution can forge a state, how a brotherhood governs, and a second, Punjab-sized answer to the century's question — who inherits the Mughals?
steps: The takeaway first: the Sikhs were the eighteenth century's proof that a community — not a province, not a governor, not even a king at the start — could rise from persecution into sovereignty: founded as a fighting…
Supporting argument 1 — the FOUNDATION: the Khalsa turned a faith into a fraternity with a political spine.

GURU GOBIND SINGH, tenth Guru from 1675 (his father, Guru Tegh Bahadur, executed at Delhi in 1675 for defying forced conversion), summoned the KHALSA at ANANDPUR on the Baisakhi of 1699: a baptised order — the five…

Two years of war with the hill rajas and the Mughal command followed; in December 1704 the Guru's fortress fell — his elder sons AJIT SINGH and JUJHAR SINGH died fighting at CHAMKAUR, and his two younger boys, ZORAWAR…

In 1708, at Nanded in the Deccan, the Guru died of an assassin's wound, and his last arrangement was the century's hinge: no successor as living Guru — the Guru-granth and the Guru-panth, scripture and community, would…
Bank the mechanism: a brotherhood that owns its own authority cannot be beheaded by arresting a head.

cards.title: The Other Half of the Rising-Powers Pair — this node's subject…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The Other Half of the Rising-Powers Pair — this node's subject — completes the roster the century's vacuum produced, in two stories. STORY ONE — MYSORE, THE MILITARY STATE: the third origin-type in this chapter (after the governor-inheritances of 03_003 and the rising-from-below powers of 03_004–03_005): a soldier's USURPATION from inside a kingdom's own army. HYDER ALI — born a minor officer (c. 1721), promoted purely by battlefield merit — became de facto ruler of MYSORE in 1761, keeping the Wodeyar rajas as nominal puppets; he built India's first Western-modelled standing army on European drill (with French advisers), taxed and traded through the state, and fought the English East India Company's expansion to a draw in the FIRST ANGLO-MYSORE WAR (1767–69, closed by the Treaty of Madras, 1769). His son TIPU SULTAN (ruled 1782–1799) — the "Tiger of Mysore" by tradition's epithet — went further: iron-cased MYSOREAN ROCKETS, state silk and steel industries, a embassy to Louis XVI's France (1787), and three more wars with the Company — the SECOND (1780–84, the disaster at Pollilur for the Company, closed by the Treaty of Mangalore, 1784), the THIRD (1790–92, the Triple Alliance of Company, Marathas and Nizam against him; the Treaty of Seringapatam 1792 taking half his kingdom and his two sons as hostages), and the FOURTH (1799), in which Seringapatam was stormed (4 May 1799) and Tipu died fighting on its walls. STORY TWO — THE MARATHA REVIVAL: the repair of 03_004's broken confederacy. MADHAVRAO I (Peshwa 1761–1772) restored Pune's command — beating the Nizam (Rakshasbhuvan, 1763) and forcing Hyder Ali to tribute (the campaigns of the 1760s–1771); NANA FADNAVIS, the minister-brain of the regency after Madhavrao's early death, ran the confederacy's politics for a generation; MAHADJI SCINDIA (d. 1794) carried the revival north — escorting the emperor SHAH ALAM II back to Delhi under Maratha protection (1771), being named the emperor's regent-plenipotentiary (Vakil-ul-Mutlaq, 1784), and re-drilling Maratha infantry with European officers (de Boigne's brigades) — so that by the Treaty of SALBAI (1782, ending the First Anglo-Maratha War in a draw) the Marathas were again the strongest power in India. WHAT THE NODE TEACHES: the two remaining answers Indian genius gave to the Mughal vacuum — the soldier's state and the repaired confederacy — and why both met the same rising rival from the sea (03_007).
steps: The takeaway first: the century's last two Indian answers — Mysore's soldier-state and the repaired Maratha confederacy — prove that the vacuum could still be answered by talent in 1761 as it had been answered in 1717…
Supporting argument 1 — MYSORE'S ORIGIN: the third way to power.
Every state this chapter has taught rose by inheriting a province (the Nizam, the Nawabs of 03_003) or by rising from a people (the Marathas, the Sikhs);
Mysore rose by USURPATION from inside — an officer became the state.

HYDER ALI, born a minor soldier's son (c. 1721), climbed by pure professional merit through Mysore's army — the Wodeyar kingdom's artillery and cavalry — until, amid the kingdom's wars with its neighbours, he held the…

REASONING: Explain why the First Anglo-Mysore War ended in the Company's concession (Treaty of Madras, 1769) and the Second in an even draw (Treaty of Mangalore, 1784) — what did….

cards.title: The Rise of the English East India Company is the chapter's final rising power…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The Rise of the English East India Company is the chapter's final rising power and its strangest — not a people, not a dynasty, not a governor, but a CORPORATION that succeeded the Mughal Empire in Bengal by conspiracy, arms and signature, in the twelve years 1757–1765. THE ORIGINS: chartered in 1600 (under Queen Elizabeth I) to carry the eastern trade, the Company built its FACTORIES (trading posts) — SURAT on the west coast (1612, after defeating the Portuguese at sea off Swally), MADRAS with Fort St. George (1639), BOMBAY (1668, received from the crown), CALCUTTA with Fort William (1690) — and, the master-paper of its first century, the imperial FARMAN OF 1717, by which the puppet-emperor FARRUKHSIYAR granted duty-free trade in Bengal: the privilege that made the Company Bengal's most privileged merchant and, in time, its most dangerous tenant. THE CONQUEST IN THREE ACTS: (1) PLASSEY (23 June 1757) — the young Nawab of Bengal SIRAJ-UD-DAULA, who had seized Calcutta (1756) in a quarrel over the Company's fortifications and privileges, was defeated by ROBERT CLIVE's small army because the Nawab's general MIR JAFAR and Bengal's great bankers (the JAGAT SETH house) had sold the battle in advance: a conspiracy-battle barely fought, which made Mir Jafar the Company's puppet Nawab and paid the Company and its officers princely sums; (2) BUXAR (22 October 1764) — the REAL battle: MIR QASIM (Mir Jafar's son-in-law, installed 1760, deposed 1763 for resisting the Company's private trade), allied with Awadh's SHUJA-UD-DAULA and the emperor SHAH ALAM II himself, met MAJOR MUNRO's Company army and lost in a day — three powers broken on one field; (3) THE DIWANI (1765) — by the Treaty of Allahabad the defeated emperor granted the Company the DIWANI — the right to collect the REVENUE of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa: the Company became the Mughal Empire's own tax-collector in its richest provinces, ruling first through a DUAL GOVERNMENT (the Company took the money; the Nawab's officials took the blame, 1765–1772) whose monstrous harvest was the GREAT FAMINE OF BENGAL (1770), before WARREN HASTINGS ended the sham (1772) and the Company governed openly. WHAT THE NODE TEACHES: the ladder from warehouse to tax-office, the three instruments that won it (sea-power and credit, the sepoy army, the divided politics of India), and the answer the century finally gave to its own question — the Mughal vacuum would be filled not by the Marathas, the Sikhs or Mysore, but by a joint-stock company with an empire's revenues and a merchant's ledger.
steps: The takeaway first: the East India Company answered the century's question — "who inherits the Mughals?" — the only way the century itself had prepared: it was granted legitimacy by a captive emperor (the Diwani, 1765)…
Supporting argument 1 — the LONG SHADOW OF THE WAREHOUSE: a century and a half of trade built the launching-pad.

The Company was chartered in 1600 and spent its first century exactly as its charter said — trading: SURAT (1612, after the sea-victory over the Portuguese at Swally proved Europe's ocean-power was transferable), MADRAS…

The master-stroke was paper: the FARMAN OF 1717, extracted from the puppet-emperor FARRUKHSIYAR's court (the same broken regency, note, that signed away chauth to the Marathas two years later), granting DUTY-FREE TRADE…
Bank the sequence: first the warehouse, then the land, then the paper — the Company was a century old in Bengal before it ever fought a battle there.
Supporting argument 2 — PLASSEY (23 June 1757): the battle that was bought.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., dating the farman to 1600 "because that is when the Company was chartered") reveals the misconception of the charter-farman merge — the 1600 charter was the English crown's paper creating the Company; the 1717 farman was the MUGHAL…

REASONING: Explain why Plassey (1757), a battle in which almost none of Siraj-ud-Daula's numerically superior army was defeated in the field, is nevertheless treated as the….
EVALUATE: "Plassey was a betrayal….

cards.title: India in the 18th Century — the Synthesis is the chapter's closing node…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: India in the 18th Century — the Synthesis is the chapter's closing node: the assembly of the seven stations into ONE causal machine, the master-tables the whole chapter can be revised from, and the exam-patterns it generates. THE CHAIN, IN FIVE LINKS: (1) THE CENTRE FAILS — the later Mughals' succession wars, the mansab–jagir decay, Aurangzeb's contested Deccan legacy (03_002); (2) THE VACUUM OPENS — Nadir Shah (1739) and Abdali (1747–1761) turn decline into collapse and empty the provinces of protection (03_002); (3) THE CLAIMANTS RISE, IN THREE TYPES — governor-inheritances (Bengal 1717, Awadh 1722, Hyderabad 1724 — 03_003), rising-from-below peoples (the Maratha confederacy to Panipat 1761 — 03_004; the Sikhs from the Khalsa 1699 to Ranjit Singh's Lahore 1799, with the Jats and Rohillas — 03_005), and the soldier-usurpation (Mysore under Hyder Ali from 1761 and Tipu Sultan to 1799), beside the Maratha revival (Madhavrao I, Nana Fadnavis, Mahadji Scindia; the draw-treaties Salbai 1782 and Mangalore 1784) — 03_006; (4) THE CORPORATION COMPOUNDS — the Company from privileged merchant (farman 1717) through the bought battle (Plassey 23 June 1757) and the field-verdict (Buxar 22 October 1764) to the signature (the Diwani 1765), the dual government and the famine of 1770 (03_007); (5) THE VERDICT SETTLES SLOWLY — by the century's end the Company holds Bengal's revenues and the coast-towns, the Marathas hold the interior's widest empire, the Sikhs hold the Punjab's new kingdom, Mysore has fallen, and the next century is the story of their collision (Chapter 04 onward). THE MASTER-TABLES this node drills: the three origin-types (inheritance / rising-from-below / usurpation) with founders and dates; the four revenue-engines (chauth, the rakhi, the puppet-tribute, the Diwani) ranked by their compounding power; and the eight-date spine (1707, 1717, 1739, 1757, 1761, 1764, 1765, 1799) that every answer hangs from. WHAT THE NODE TEACHES: not new facts but the CONNECTIONS — how each node's mechanism fed the next, which judgments the chapter's marks live in, and how to write the synthesis answers the exam actually asks.
steps: The takeaway first: the eighteenth century is one machine, not eight topics: a failing centre opened a vacuum; the vacuum was answered by every kind of climber — governors, peoples, soldiers, and finally a corporation …
Supporting argument 1 — THE CHAIN ASSEMBLED: how each station causes the next.

Recite it with its dated hinges: AURANGZEB dies (1707) → the succession wars and the mansab–jagir spiral rot the centre (03_002) → the provinces stop obeying and start INHERITING (Bengal 1717, Awadh 1722, Hyderabad 1724…
Abdali to 1761 — the Punjab emptied for the Khalsa, the Marathas broken at Panipat) → the vacuum's second generation rises (the misls;

Hyder's usurpation 1761; the Maratha revival) → and while every Indian climber fights every other, the Company converts a warehouse into a tax-office (Plassey 1757, Buxar 1764, the Diwani 1765) — the chain's one dirty…
Exam-use: any "trace the events" answer is this chain with dates; any "why" answer is this chain with one link highlighted.

REASONING: Assemble the chapter's causal chain in five links, and show at each link how the failing centre — directly or by licence — enabled the climbers: name the paper or the….
EVALUATE: "The greatest state-builder of the eighteenth century was not a king at all." Weigh the claim: who is the sentence pointing to, what did they build that no monarch of….

cards.title: Traders to Rulers — the chapter overview is the map-station…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: Traders to Rulers — the chapter overview is the map-station: the frame on which the chapter's seven stations hang. THE ARC, IN FOUR PHASES: (1) THE TRADING PHASE (1600–1740s) — the English East India Company chartered (1600), its factories planted (Surat 1613; Madras 1639; Bombay 1668; Calcutta 1690), its privileges papered (Jahangir's farman 1615; the Bengal duty-free farman 1717) — a merchant among merchants, buying with silver, fighting only for its warehouses (04_002's station). (2) THE CONQUEST PHASE (1756–1765) — the privileges-quarrel detonates in Bengal: Plassey (23 June 1757, the conspiracy-battle against Siraj-ud-Daula), the puppet-Nawabs, Buxar (22 October 1764, the real field-victory over Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula and Shah Alam II), and the Diwani (1765) — the Company becomes the revenue-master of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa (04_003's station). (3) THE ADMINISTRATION-AND-EXPANSION PHASE (1772–1798) — the Company must govern what it has looted: the dual government ended (1772), revenue-systems invented (Cornwallis's Permanent Settlement, 1793), and the appetite grown: Wellesley's SUBSIDIARY ALLIANCE system (from 1798) and the wars that fed it — Mysore finished (Seringapatam, 4 May 1799), the Marathas broken in two wars (1803–05) (04_004–04_005's stations). (4) THE COMPLETION PHASE (1799–1856) — the map closed: Sind (1843), the Punjab (the Anglo-Sikh wars 1845–46 and 1848–49, annexed 1849), the Doctrine of Lapse (Dalhousie, from 1848) swallowing adopted-heir states, Awadh annexed (1856) — leaving a Company-State whose exactions and discontents arm the next chapter's storm (04_006–04_007's stations), before the chapter's synthesis drills the exam patterns (04_008). WHAT THIS NODE TEACHES: the arc's logic (every conquest paid for the next), the phase-map and its dates, the chapter's master-question (how did a trading corporation become the sovereign of India — and what did India pay for it?), and the study-method for the whole chapter.
steps: The takeaway first: this chapter is one mechanism wearing four costumes: a company whose conquests paid for themselves could never stop conquering — privilege made it rich (1600–1740s), a quarrel made it sovereign…
Supporting argument 1 — PHASE ONE, THE TRADING PHASE (1600–1740s): the warehouse century.

The Company was chartered (1600) as a MONOPOLY of English eastern trade, and its first Indian century was exactly what its charter said: factories (trading posts) at SURAT (1613, under Jahangir's farman of 1615), MADRAS…

The phase's master-paper was the Bengal duty-free FARMAN (1717), extracted from a weakening court: the privilege that made the Company Bengal's richest merchant — and planted the quarrel that would end the phase.
Exam-logic of the phase: trade succeeded because it stayed SMALL — forts for guards, not conquests; the Company of 1740 had no intention of ruling anyone.
(Full detail: 04_002.) Supporting argument 2 — PHASE TWO, THE CONQUEST PHASE (1756–1765): sovereignty by accident and appetite.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "the phases link because the British planned from 1600 to conquer India step by step") reveals the misconception of the blueprint-reading — the ladder was built by accumulation, not by a master-plan: no director in London in 1600 foresaw…

REASONING: Explain why the acquisition of the Diwani (1765) — a paper transaction with no battle — is nevertheless the chapter's TRUE hinge, more transformative than Plassey….
EVALUATE: "The subsidiary alliance was conquest by ledger." Weigh the sentence against the older method (open war and annexation): what the alliance-system achieved that armies….

cards.title: The English East India Company (EIC) was a joint‑stock company chartered by…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The English East India Company (EIC) was a joint‑stock company chartered by Queen Elizabeth I on 31 December 1600 to pursue trade with the East Indies. In India its primary aim was commercial: securing cotton textiles, silk, indigo, saltpetre and spices for European markets. The Company operated through “factories” — fortified warehouses cum offices — established at Surat (1613), Madras (1639, Fort St George), Bombay (1668, received as part of Catherine of Braganza’s dowry) and Calcutta (1690, Fort William). A crucial diplomatic breakthrough came in 1615 when Emperor Jahangir issued a farman granting the EIC duty‑free trade and the right to establish factories in Mughal territories. The Company’s trade was conducted under the “factory system” where factors (agents) negotiated with local merchants, maintained accounts in Persian and kept armed guards for protection. Profits were repatriated to London shareholders, and the Company’s growing revenue enabled it to raise private armies, intervene in local succession disputes and eventually acquire territorial revenue rights (diwani) after the Battle of Plassey (1757). This node covers only the trade phase: charter, early factories, Mughal farmans, commodities, and the commercial mechanisms that laid the financial foundation for later political expansion.
steps: The English East India Company began as a profit‑driven trading corporation, not a political power.
Here is why: its royal charter of 1600 gave it a monopoly on English trade east of the Cape of Good Hope, but it had to negotiate access with Indian rulers.
First, the Company secured a foothold at Surat in 1613 after defeating the Portuguese in a naval skirmish, showing that military force could protect commerce.
Second, Emperor Jahangir’s 1615 farman granted duty‑free trade and the right to establish factories, turning a precarious presence into a legally recognised enterprise.
Third, the Company replicated the factory model at Madras (1639), Bombay (1668) and Calcutta (1690), each strategically placed near textile‑producing regions and maritime routes.

Fourth, the factory system employed factors who advanced money to Indian weavers (dadni system), collected finished cloth, and shipped it to London in exchange for silver, creating a triangular flow of goods and bullion.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 1613) reveals the misconception that the first factory’s founding year is the same as the charter date — confusing operational start with legal incorporation.
remember: What year was the English East India Company granted its royal charter by Queen Elizabeth I.
Why was the farman issued by Emperor Jahangir in 1615 a turning point for the Company’s trade in India.
Evaluate the statement: “The English East India Company’s early factories were primarily military forts.”.

cards.title: The conquest phase of the English East India Company (EIC) refers to the period…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The conquest phase of the English East India Company (EIC) refers to the period (mid‑18th century – early 19th century) when the Company transformed from a commercial enterprise into a territorial power through military victories, diplomatic treaties, and strategic alliances. Key sub‑concepts include: 1. Military engagements – decisive battles where EIC forces, often led by British officers and Indian sepoys, defeated regional powers (e.g., Battle of Plassey 1757 against Nawab Siraj‑ud‑Daula of Bengal; Battle of Buxar 1764 against the combined forces of Mir Qasim, Shuja‑ud‑Daula, and the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II). 2. Treaties and grants – legal instruments that converted battlefield success into revenue rights and political control (e.g., Treaty of Allahabad 1765 granting Diwani of Bengal, Bihar, Orissa). 3. Use of Indian allies and rivalries – the Company exploited succession disputes (e.g., supporting Mir Jafar at Plassey) and played off Maratha, Mysore, and Mughal factions. 4. Institutionalisation of military power – creation of the Presidency armies (Bengal, Madras, Bombay) and the post of Commander‑in‑Chief, giving the Company a standing force independent of the Crown. Together these elements turned trade privileges into sovereign‑like authority over territory, revenue, and administration, setting the stage for the later “expansion to rule” phase.
steps: The conquest of India by the English East India Company was not a single event but a chain of calculated military victories that turned commercial footholds into territorial sovereignty.
Here is why: the Company’s private armies, superior artillery, and ability to exploit Indian political fragmentation gave it a decisive edge.
First, the Battle of Plassey (23 June 1757) saw Robert Clive’s 3,000‑strong force defeat Nawab Siraj‑ud‑Daula’s 50,000 men because Mir Jafar, the Nawab’s commander, secretly allied with Clive.
The victory gave the EIC control of Bengal’s vast revenue, formalised by the Treaty of Allahabad (1765) where Mughal emperor Shah Alam II granted the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.
Second, the Battle of Buxar (22 October 1764) pitted the Company’s 7,000 troops under Hector Munro against the combined armies of Mir Qasim (Bengal), Shuja‑ud‑Daula (Awadh), and the Mughal emperor.

The EIC’s disciplined volleys and field artillery shattered the coalition, leading to the Treaty of Allahabad (1765) again, this time confirming the Diwani and extracting heavy indemnities from Awadh.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Battle of Buxar”) reveals the misconception that the later, larger battle was the first, confusing chronology and the sequence of conquest.
remember: Which battle in 1757 marked the English East India Company’s first major military victory in Bengal.
Explain why the English East India Company was able to defeat the much larger army of Nawab Siraj‑ud‑Daula at Plassey.
Assess the significance of the Treaty of Allahabad (1765) for the Company’s transformation from trader to ruler.

cards.title: Expansion to Rule — the Company builds a government is this chapter's…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: Expansion to Rule — the Company builds a government is this chapter's machine-room: how the conquered territories (04_003's stations) were administered, how the revenue-systems were invented, and how rule expanded beyond Bengal. THE ADMINISTRATIVE SPINE: WARREN HASTINGS (Governor-General from 1773 under the Regulating Act — the first office-holder with a council) ended the DUAL GOVERNMENT (1772), brought the revenue-collection under the Company's own officers, and began the judicial experiments (district courts, a Supreme Court at Calcutta, 1774, under the same Act); LORD CORNWALLIS (1786–93) systematised everything — separating revenue from justice (the COLLECTOR stripped of judicial powers, district judges and courts of appeal erected, the CORNWALLIS CODE, 1793), professionalising the CIVIL SERVICE (salaried, no-private-trade covenanted officers, 1793), organising the POLICE (the thana system under a Superintendent of Police in each district), and completing the great revenue-deed: the PERMANENT SETTLEMENT (1793 — the decennial settlement of 1790 made perpetual), by which the ZAMINDARS of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa were recognised as PROPRIETORS of their estates, the revenue FIXED IN PERPETUITY, and default punished by the "sunset law" (pay by sunset or the estate is auctioned). THE ALTERNATIVE SETTLEMENTS: the RYOTWARI system — settlement DIRECT with each cultivating RYOT, periodically reassessed — introduced in the Madras Presidency by THOMAS MUNRO (from the Baramahal experiments of 1792, systematised from the 1810s–20s) and extended in Bombay; and the MAHALWARI system — settlement with the VILLAGE ESTATE (the mahal) as a joint unit — in the North-Western Provinces (from 1822, revised 1833). THE EXPANSION BEYOND BENGAL: the three PRESIDENCIES (Bengal, Madras, Bombay) grew their own armies and territories; the southern wars (Mysore) and the western advances made the revenue-machine a subcontinental one — until WELLESLEY's subsidiary system (04_005's station) turned expansion into a standing method. WHAT THE NODE TEACHES: the machine's logic (revenue first, justice and police to protect it), the three settlements as three bets on who should carry the land-tax (the zamindar, the ryot, the village), and the consequences each carried for the peasant underneath them.
steps: The takeaway first: the Company-State was built by crisis in a fixed order — the famine of 1770 shamed it into governing, the Regulating Act (1773) framed the government, and Cornwallis (1793) froze the machine into its…
Supporting argument 1 — THE CRISIS THAT BUILT THE MACHINE: why the merchant had to become government.

The Diwani (1765) gave the Company Bengal's revenue but the DUAL GOVERNMENT gave it no responsibility: the Company collected, the Nawab's deputy governed, and when the drought of 1770 met that accountability-vacuum, the…
The lesson went into the machine's foundation: revenue without governance destroys revenue.

So HASTINGS (Governor-General from 1773 under the REGULATING ACT, with a council of four; the same Act erected the SUPREME COURT at Calcutta, 1774) ended the dual system (1772), collected through the Company's own…

cards.title: From Trade to Territory — Wellesley's Subsidiary System is this chapter's…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: From Trade to Territory — Wellesley's Subsidiary System is this chapter's expansion-method station: how the Company, between 1798 and 1805, made itself the paramount power of India less by fighting new conquests than by making Indian states pay for, house and obey the army that ended their independence. THE ARCHITECT: RICHARD WELLESLEY (Lord Mornington), GOVERNOR-GENERAL from 1798 to 1805, arriving in the year Napoleon's expedition reached Egypt (1798) — the French threat (Tipu Sultan's French connections at Mysore; French officers in Indian courts) was his stated alarm, and PARAMOUNTCY — the Company above every Indian power — his open aim. THE INSTRUMENT, THE SUBSIDIARY ALLIANCE (treaties from 1798 onward), had four load-bearing terms: (1) the state accepted COMPANY TROOPS stationed permanently in its territory, at the STATE'S EXPENSE — paid in cash or, when the treasury failed, by CESSION OF TERRITORY in lieu of payment (Hyderabad's "Ceded Districts", 1800; Awadh's cession of Rohilkhand and about half its lands, 1801); (2) the state DISBANDED or cut down its own army and agreed to admit no other EUROPEANS (in practice: expel the French) without the Company's consent; (3) the state gave up its EXTERNAL INDEPENDENCE — no war, no negotiation, no embassy with any other power except through the Company, and disputes with neighbours referred to Company arbitration; (4) the state received a BRITISH RESIDENT at its court — the Company's political agent, the treaty's living supervisor. The ruler kept his throne, his court and his internal revenue-collection — the shell of kingship; the reality of sovereignty (defence, diplomacy, and increasingly internal interference) passed to Calcutta. THE WARS THAT COMPLETED THE NET: the FOURTH ANGLO-MYSORE WAR (1799) — Tipu Sultan, the one great ruler who refused, killed fighting at the storming of SRIRANGAPATNA (4 May 1799); Mysore was carved up — territory to the Company and the Nizam, the old Hindu WODEYAR dynasty restored as rulers under a subsidiary treaty. The SECOND ANGLO-MARATHA WAR (1803–05) followed the Peshwa BAJI RAO II's flight to Company protection and the TREATY OF BASSEIN (31 December 1802) — the Peshwa accepted the subsidiary terms; Sindhia and Bhonsle refused and were defeated (ASSAYE, 23 September 1803, and Argaon and Gawilgarh under ARTHUR WELLESLEY, the Governor-General's brother; DELHI and LASWARI, 1803, under GERARD LAKE; the treaties of DEOGAON and SURJI-ANJANGAON, December 1803), while HOLKAR kept the war alive through 1804–05 (Monson's famous retreat) before peace in 1805. THE RESULT: by 1805 the Company was the acknowledged paramount power from the coasts to Delhi — the map turned Company-coloured by signature and siege together, and the appetite-law of 04_004 (administration needs revenue, revenue needs territory) had found its cheapest engine: the states themselves financed the machine that absorbed them.

He also inherited the appetite-law of 04_004: the Company-State's growing payroll demanded revenue, revenue demanded territory, and open war for every district was ruinously slow.

cards.title: The Final Annexations — from paramountcy to dominion is this chapter's…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The Final Annexations — from paramountcy to dominion is this chapter's completion-station: how the Company, between 1805 and 1856, converted Wellesley's network of protected states (04_005) into outright possession — ending the treaty-shells and colouring the map Company-owned. THE INTERLUDE (1805–1813): after Wellesley's recall his successors (Cornwallis's last brief term, then Barlow and Minto) practised NON-INTERVENTION — the Directors feared the cost; the net, not the map, grew. THE FINISH OF THE MARATHAS: the THIRD ANGLO-MARATHA WAR (1817–18) under LORD HASTINGS — the Pindari hunt drew the confederacy's chiefs to arms (Baji Rao II attacked at Kirkee; the Nagpur Bhonsle at Sitabuldi; Holkar beaten at MAHIDPUR); the Peshwa surrendered (1818) and was pensioned to Bithur near Kanpur; the PESHWSHIP WAS ABOLISHED, Poona annexed, and the Maratha confederacy — the last great Indian land-power of the centre — was struck off the map. THE WAR-ANNEXATIONS OF THE NORTH-WEST: SINDH (1843) — the Amirs' state taken after Sir Charles Napier's victories at MIANI and Hyderabad (Dubbo), under Governor-General Ellenborough, in the wake of the First Afghan disaster (the retreat from Kabul, 1842) and Indus-frontier logic; the famous "Peccavi" pun ("I have sinned/Sindh") attached to Napier is almost certainly a journalist's invention — treat it as apocryphal. THE PUNJAB (1845–49): Ranjit Singh's Sikh kingdom — the one Indian power rebuilt to face the Company (its treaty of Amritsar, 1809, fixing the Sutlej as the boundary) — fell apart after his death (1839) in four years of palace murders; the FIRST ANGLO-SIKH WAR (1845–46: Mudki, Ferozeshah, Aliwal, Sobraon) ended with the Treaty of Lahore (1846 — indemnity, cessions, Kashmir sold to Gulab Singh of Jammu, a British Resident at Lahore under the boy-king Duleep Singh); the SECOND (1848–49: Chilianwala — a battle the Company nearly lost — and Gujrat, the decisive victory) ended with the ANNEXATION OF THE PUNJAB (29 March 1849) under LORD DALHOUSIE: Duleep Singh pensioned and deposed, the Koh-i-noor surrendered to Queen Victoria. THE DOCTRINE OF LAPSE (applied systematically by DALHOUSIE, Governor-General 1848–56): the rule that when a ruler of a protected (dependent) state died WITHOUT A NATURAL MALE HEIR, an adopted son could not succeed without the paramount power's consent — and without it the state "lapsed" to the Company; the principle was older than Dalhousie (governments had refused adoptions before), but he applied it as a SYSTEM: SATARA (1848 — the flagship case), Jaitpur and Sambalpur (1849), Baghat (1850), Udaipur (1852 — later restored), JHANSI (1853 — the adopted heir of Gangadhar Rao refused, and the RANI LAKSHMIBAI's petitions rejected), NAGPUR (1854 — the last and largest). THE MISGOVERNMENT ANNEXATION: AWADH (1856) — NOT a lapse case (the Nawab had heirs): Wajid Ali Shah was deposed and the kingdom annexed on the declared ground of chronic "misgovernment" — the official finding standing on official reports, the historians' reading (revenue-hunger and garrison-logic) standing beside it; both are given here. THE RESULT: by 1856 the Company ruled directly from Bengal to the Sutlej and beyond, and the annexations had manufactured a class of exact, personal, remembered grievances — the deposed Rani of Jhansi, the dispossessed taluqdars of Awadh, the sepoys' own homeland, the Nana Sahib's stopped pension — which are 04_007's storm-material.

cards.title: The Company-State — Government Built and Discontents Stored is this chapter's…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The Company-State — Government Built and Discontents Stored is this chapter's structure-and-tension station: the constitutional machine that had evolved from a trading body into a sovereign government, and the four-column ledger of grievances stored under its floors by 1856. THE STRUCTURE, LONDON END: a DOUBLE GOVERNMENT — the COMPANY's own organs (the COURT OF PROPRIETORS — the shareholders; the COURT OF DIRECTORS, twenty-four, managing commerce and patronage) alongside PARLIAMENT's control, built act by act: the REGULATING ACT (1773 — the Governor-General-in-Council; parliamentary oversight begins), PITT'S INDIA ACT (1784 — the BOARD OF CONTROL, six members, taking political affairs while the Directors kept trade: a merchant-body under a state-bridle), and the CHARTER ACTS — 1813 (the Company's INDIA TRADE MONOPOLY ended, except the tea-trade with China; missionaries admitted; an annual education-grant of one lakh of rupees asserted), 1833 (the Company's COMMERCIAL FUNCTIONS ENDED ENTIRELY — it became a purely administrative trustee; the Governor-General of BENGAL became GOVERNOR-GENERAL OF INDIA — William Bentinck the first; a Law Commission under Macaulay to codify), and 1853 (the Company's tenure made a trust without fixed term; the legislative and executive functions of the Council separated; the CIVIL SERVICE opened to COMPETITION). THE STRUCTURE, INDIA END: the GOVERNOR-GENERAL-IN-COUNCIL at Calcutta supreme over the three PRESIDENCIES (Bengal, Madras, Bombay — each with its Governor and its army), the Presidency-governments subordinated (1773/1784), and the DISTRICT machine below (04_004's Collector, judge, thana) — the file that ran from a village account to London. THE ARMY: three PRESIDENCY ARMIES of sepoys — Indian soldiers under British officers — the Bengal army the largest, recruited heavily from the high-caste peasantry of AWADH and Bihar: the state's real muscle, and — as the events after this chapter showed — its standing structural risk. THE REFORM-FACE: the "trusteeship" idea (rule for the governed's improvement) legislated from BENTINCK's decade — the abolition of SATI (1829), Macaulay's EDUCATION MINUTE (1835, English as the medium of advance), Wood's Despatch (1854, the education-charter), the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act (1856) — genuine measures, passed WITHOUT CONSULTATION of the governed, in the same decades the Charter Act of 1813 had opened India to MISSIONARY societies. THE DISCONTENT-LEDGER, four columns: (1) ECONOMIC — the DRAIN (Home Charges: dividends, interest, pensions, the establishment's cost in England — the later "drain theory" of Dadabhai Naoroji named it), the decline of the artisan-export trades (the Company's contract-binding of weavers; then machine-cloth from Britain undercutting handloom), and the peasant's revenue-and-debt squeeze (04_004's settlements); (2) POLITICAL — 04_006's annexation-ledger: dispossessed rulers, stopped pensions (Jhansi's Rani; the Nana Sahib), Awadh's taluqdars; (3) SOCIO-RELIGIOUS — the fear that reform was conversion's opening (missionaries from 1813; the Religious Disabilities Act 1850 read as favouring converts; reform-laws imposed without asking); (4) MILITARY — sepoy grievances: stagnant pay against growing duties, the Post Office Act (1854, ending their free postage), the GENERAL SERVICE ENLISTMENT ACT (1856, obliging new recruits to serve overseas — read as caste-loss), and finally the greased-cartridge rumour of 1857 — the SPARK, not the cause. By 1856 the machine stood complete and the floor beneath it stood dry: that floor is what the next chapter's storm tested.

cards.title: Traders to Rulers — the Chapter Synthesis and its Examination is this chapter's…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: Traders to Rulers — the Chapter Synthesis and its Examination is this chapter's roof-station: the five-rung (plus the structure-station's sixth view) ladder composed into one narrative, one driving logic, and one exam-architecture. THE LADDER, RESTATED IN FULL: RUNG 1 — THE TRADE-STATION (04_002): the East India Company chartered (1600), the factories and fortifications (Surat, Madras, Bombay, Calcutta), the Mughal Grants and farman-system, the French rival's arrival — merchants under Mughal permission; RUNG 2 — THE CONQUEST-STATION (04_003): the Carnatic contests and the battle-field turns — PLASSEY (1757: conspiracy, a bribed commander, an unshared victory), BUXAR (1764: the real military verdict against three allied powers), the DIWANI (1765: the revenue-right of Bengal-Bihar-Orissa by treaty-deed) — trade's guardians become revenue's lords; RUNG 3 — THE MACHINE-STATION (04_004): the crisis-built administration — dual government ended (1772), the Regulating Act's frame (1773), the Supreme Court (1774), Cornwallis's separation and Code (1793), the salaried covenanted service, the thana-police, and the three revenue-settlements (Permanent 1793; Ryotwari — Munro's Madras and Bombay; Mahalwari — NWP 1822/1833) with the district-machine (Collector, judge, thana) and the appetite-law; RUNG 4 — THE SUBSIDIARY-STATION (04_005): Wellesley's system (from 1798) — the four terms (troops at the state's expense, army cut and other Europeans expelled, diplomacy surrendered, Resident installed), the cession-arithmetic (Ceded Districts 1800; Awadh's half 1801), the enforcing wars (Srirangapatna 1799; Bassein 1802; Assaye, Delhi, Laswari and the December-1803 treaties; Holkar to 1805) and paramountcy south of the Sutlej; RUNG 5 — THE COMPLETION-STATION (04_006): the final annexations — the Maratha finish (1817–18, Peshwaship abolished), Sindh (1843), the two Sikh wars and the Punjab (1845–49), the Doctrine of Lapse applied (Satara 1848, Jhansi 1853, Nagpur 1854), Awadh on "misgovernment" (1856); THE STRUCTURE-VIEW (04_007): the finished Company-State — Parliament's bridle (Board of Control 1784; Charter Acts 1813/1833/1853), the Governor-General-in-Council, the subordinated Presidencies, the sepoy armies — standing on the four-column grievance-ledger (economic, political, socio-religious, military) with the spark-vs-causes logic for the storm beyond this chapter. THE DRIVING LOGIC (the synthesis' one sentence): each rung's GAIN became the next rung's INSTRUMENT — the revenue paid the sepoy, the sepoy enforced the treaty, the treaty created the paramountcy, the paramountcy powered the files, the files completed the dominion — no step aimed at the destination; the destination emerged from steps. THE EXAM-ARCHITECTURE: this chapter is examined in six question-forms — (i) TERM-DEFINITIONS with dates (Diwani, subsidiary alliance, Doctrine of Lapse, sunset-law); (ii) CHRONOLOGY arrangements; (iii) CAUSE–EFFECT chains (why Plassey mattered; why the subsidiary system expanded the empire); (iv) TABLES (the settlements-grid, the treaty-ledger, the grounds-table); (v) PERSON-and-STATE questions (Clive, Tipu, Ranjit Singh, Dalhousie, the Rani); and (vi) ASSESS-judgments (empire-by-design or by accident; legality versus legitimacy; spark versus causes) — and this node drills one template for each.

cards.title: British Policies and Impacts — the chapter-map is this chapter's…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: British Policies and Impacts — the chapter-map is this chapter's overview-station: the survey of what the colonial government (Crown rule after 1858, carrying forward the Company's inheritance) DID to India across three policy-domains, what each policy DID TO the people living under it, and how Indians RESPONDED — so that every later node's detail has a shelf to sit on. THE THREE DOMAINS: (1) THE ECONOMIC DOMAIN — the land-revenue systems' demands (04_004's settlements as lived), the ruin of handicrafts and the one-way trade (raw materials out, machine-cloth in), the DRAIN OF WEALTH (the Home Charges — the annual flow of taxes, dividends, pensions and costs to Britain, named and numbered by DADABHAI NAOROJI), the commercialisation of agriculture (cash-crops like indigo and cotton replacing food), railways and their double face (integration and market-forcing), and the famine-decades (the Great Famine of 1876–78 as the emblem) — economic policies whose IMPACT is measured in villages, looms and empty granaries; (2) THE ADMINISTRATIVE DOMAIN — the Crown's takeover (Government of India Act, 1858; the Secretary of State; the Viceroy), Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1858) and its promises, the legal codes (the Indian Penal Code, 1860; the Criminal Procedure Code, 1861), the Police Act (1861), the Indian Civil Service as the "steel frame" (recruited by examination in London; Indians admitted in principle, barred in practice), the army reorganised on "martial classes" logic after 1857 — administration as the machine of a state that governed WITHOUT consent; (3) THE EDUCATIONAL DOMAIN — Macaulay's Minute (1835) and English as the ladder, Wood's Despatch (1854, the "Magna Carta" of Indian education), the universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras (1857), the Hunter Commission (1882) — education producing the English-knowing middle class that would staff the system and, in time, argue it into history. THE RESPONSE-THREAD: EARLY RESISTANCE — the tribal and peasant risings the policy-decades produced (the Kol uprising, 1831–32; the SANTHAL HUL, 1855–56, under Sido and Kanhu; the Indigo Revolt, 1859–60) and the reform-and-organisation thread that grew alongside — the chapter's argument that every policy-domain minted its own resistance. THE CHAPTER'S LOGIC (why it matters): the same half-century that drained India built India's modern skeleton — law-codes, railways, a civil service, universities, an English-speaking public — and the tension between those two ledgers (the moderniser's and the exploiter's) is the examination's favourite judgment and the next century's political fuel; every node of this chapter (the policy-overview 05_002, the early risings 05_003, the fifty-references framework 05_004, the revenue-and-economy station 05_005, the administration station 05_006, the education station 05_007, the synthesis 05_008) sits somewhere on that double ledger.

cards.title: The economic, administrative and educational policies of British rule…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The economic, administrative and educational policies of British rule — and their effects is this chapter's policy-survey: the first full walk through the rulebook of Crown-rule India (the frame built by the Government of India Act, 1858), domain by domain, policy by policy, effect by effect — so that the later deep-dive stations (revenue-and-economy 05_005, administration 05_006, education 05_007) meet a student who already knows the shelves. (1) THE ECONOMIC POLICIES: the LAND-REVENUE DEMANDS — the settlements inherited from the Company (the Permanent Settlement of 1793 fixing zamindars' payments in Bengal; the Ryotwari settlement dealing directly with the cultivator in Madras and Bombay; the Mahalwari in the north-west) — run at high, rigid demands, collected on calendar dates regardless of harvest; the COMMERCIALISATION OF AGRICULTURE — cash-crops for export (indigo, cotton, jute) displacing food-grains; the ONE-WAY TRADE — raw materials out, British machine-goods in — which ruined the HANDICRAFTS (weavers, spinners, smiths) that had made Indian cloth world-famous; the DRAIN OF WEALTH — the annual "Home Charges" (interest on Indian public debt, pensions and salaries of British officials, the India Office's costs, army bills charged to India) paid out of India's export surplus without any return flow — named and measured by DADABHAI NAOROJI (his landmark "Poverty and Un-British Rule in India", 1901) and documented by RAMESH CHANDRA DUTT; the RAILWAYS (the first passenger line, Bombay to Thane, 1853) built on a guarantee-system — British investors promised interest from Indian revenues — the double-faced emblem: integration for India, profits for Britain; and the FAMINE-DECADES, of which the Great Famine of 1876–78 (millions dead in the Deccan and the south while grain moved by rail to ports) is the emblem, answered by the first Famine Commission (1880). (2) THE ADMINISTRATIVE POLICIES: the 1858 frame (Secretary of State in Council; Viceroy; Proclamation-promises); ONE LAW — the Indian Penal Code (1860, drafted in the 1830s by the First Law Commission), the codes of procedure (1861), the High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras (1862); ONE POLICE — the Police Act (1861), a constabulary built to protect the state after 1857, not to serve communities; ONE SERVICE — the Indian Civil Service, the "steel frame", recruited by competitive examination held ONLY IN LONDON (Satyendranath Tagore, passing in 1863, remained the famous exception); and the ARMY re-organised after 1857 — a higher ratio of British troops, artillery kept in European hands, recruitment steered to "martial" groups away from the uprising's heartlands. (3) THE EDUCATIONAL POLICIES: Macaulay's Minute (1835) fixing ENGLISH as the medium and the aim; the "filtration" hope that education given to the few would trickle downward; Wood's Despatch (1854) — the "Magna Carta of Indian education" — grading the ladder from vernacular schools to colleges, funding through grants-in-aid; the universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras (1857); the Hunter Commission (1882) surveying the system and pushing primary and private education. THE EFFECTS-LEDGER (the node's real subject): a peasantry pressed into the moneylender's grip and losing land to it; artisans becoming field-labourers; a narrow English-knowing middle class of clerks, lawyers, editors and teachers — created for the machine, and turning into its critics (the press, the bar, the associations, and by 1885 the Indian National Congress); and, threading all of it, the risings the policies minted (Kol 1831–32; Santhal Hul 1855–56; Indigo Revolt 1859–60 — 05_003's full story): every policy in this survey delivered a DOUBLE EFFECT — one entry built, one entry took.
steps: The takeaway first: the policies of Crown-rule India were one machine with three faces — money, order and mind — and this node's whole work is to walk that machine once through, domain by domain, because every policy…

Ryotwari with the cultivator directly in Madras and Bombay;

Mahalwari at village level in the north-west) were now run HARD — demands fixed high and collected on fixed dates, whatever the rains did. The cultivator's only escape when the crop failed was the MONEYLENDER; his…

Beside it ran the COMMERCIALISATION push: indigo in Bengal under planter-contracts, cotton booming during the American Civil War (1861–65) and crashing after, jute for the mills — export-crops replacing food-security.

cards.title: Early resistance — the tribal and peasant risings of the policy-decades is this…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: Early resistance — the tribal and peasant risings of the policy-decades is this chapter's response-station: the study of three emblem-risings, each the direct receipt of a policy walked in 05_002 — each with its cause (a specific policy-pressure), its community, its course, and its partial outcome. (1) THE KOL UPRISING (1831–32, Chota Nagpur): the adivasi communities of the Chota Nagpur region (the Oraon, Munda and Bhumij peoples, known collectively as the Kols) rose against the ALIENATION OF THEIR LAND — traders, moneylenders and settlers from outside (the "outsiders") had been squeezing into the region, grabbing land through debt and dubious titles, backed by the new British courts and tax-collectors; the rising burned the houses of moneylenders and outsiders and drove them from village after village, until British troops suppressed it (1832); its legacy included a separate administrative arrangement for the region (the South-West Frontier Agency, 1834) and, in time, the idea of protective tenancy-laws for Chota Nagpur's tribals. (2) THE SANTHAL HUL (1855–56, the Rajmahal hills): the Santhals, settled by the government in the demarcated hill-lands of the Rajmahal region (the Damin-i-Koh, demarcated in the 1830s), were destroyed by the DEBT-TRAP — moneylenders' advances at ruinous interest, zamindars demanding rent on land the Santhals had cleared, police and officials siding with the creditors; in JUNE 1855, thousands of Santhals (accounts speak of about ten thousand) gathered at BHOGNADIH and, under the brothers SIDO AND KANHU (with their brothers Chand and Bhairav, and the women leaders Phulo and Jhano also remembered), proclaimed an end to the Company's rule — the HUL (the rising) attacked moneylenders, planters' agents and railway contractors, ran its own parallel authority, and was crushed by British troops with great brutality (1855–56); its outcome included the creation of a special district — the SANTHAL PARGANAS — with protective laws restricting the transfer of Santhal land to outsiders. (3) THE INDIGO REVOLT (1859–60, Bengal): the ryots of Bengal's delta, bound to grow indigo for European planters through cash-ADVANCES that enslaved them at unfair prices and coercion (beatings, crop-destruction, burning of villages), REFUSED TO SOW indigo after the 1859 season — beginning at Govindpur in Nadia district under DIGAMBAR BISWAS and BISHNUCHARAN BISWAS — swore collective oaths, and resisted planter-force together; the revolt was unique in its ALLIES: the Bengali intelligentsia's press (the "Hindu Patriot" of Harish Chandra Mukherjee; Dinabandhu Mitra's play "NIL DARPAN", 1860, exposing planter atrocities — whose translation-trial in 1861 made the scandal public) carried the ryots' case to Bengal and to London; the government's INDIGO COMMISSION (1860) condemned the planters' oppression, the contract-law was tightened, and indigo cultivation largely COLLAPSED in Bengal (the planters moved it to Bihar). THE PATTERN (the node's argument): all three were LOCAL, POLICY-MINTED (land-alienation; debt and forest-loss; planter-coercion), ORGANISED (oaths, assemblies, parallel authority — not aimless riots), and PARTIALLY SUCCESSFUL (suppressed by force, but forcing protective measures) — and all three prove the chapter's thesis: every policy minted its own resistance, decades before the national movement (05_004 gives the framework; the 1857 uprising itself belongs to the next chapter).

So resistance aimed at the agents — burning moneylenders' account-books, refusing the planter's advances, expelling the outsiders — because the agents were the policy's visible face in the village.

And resistance was ORGANISED, not spontaneous: oaths sworn together, assemblies of thousands, parallel authorities proclaimed, refusal-co-ordinated across villages — the colonial record's word "riot" is the ruler's…
Bank the sentence: local causes, community organisation, policy-targeted force, partial concessions — the four-marker of an early rising.

cards.title: The “colonial 50 refs” is a pedagogical framework that identifies roughly fifty…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The “colonial 50 refs” is a pedagogical framework that identifies roughly fifty pivotal British legislative acts, administrative reports, educational despatches, and revenue settlements issued between 1757 and 1947. These references are clustered into three policy domains: 1. Economic policies – land revenue systems (Permanent Settlement 1793, Ryotwari 1820s, Mahalwari 1833), commercial regulations (Charter Acts 1813, 1833, 1853), and fiscal measures (Income Tax Act 1860). 2. Administrative policies – constitutional acts (Regulating Act 1773, Pitt’s India Act 1784, Charter Acts 1793, 1813, 1833, 1853, Government of India Acts 1858, 1909, 1919, 1935) and key commissions (Royal Commission on Decentralisation 1907, Simon Commission 1927). 3. Educational policies – seminal despatches and minutes (Macaulay’s Minute 1835, Wood’s Despatch 1854, Hunter Commission 1882, Sadler Commission 1917, Hartog Committee 1929). The references are interdependent: revenue from economic policies financed the administrative machinery; administrative acts created the legal space for educational despatches; and educational policies produced a class of Indian clerks who staffed the revenue and judicial departments. This node does not analyse each act in depth — that is done in sibling nodes 002 and 003 — but it supplies the master list and the conceptual links that let a student navigate the chapter’s evidence base efficiently.
steps: The “colonial 50 refs” are the fifty most cited British laws, reports, and despatches that together structured the economic, administrative, and educational framework of colonial India.
Here is why: first, the British did not rule by whim; they codified control through a paper trail of acts and reports that can be grouped into three functional families.

Second, these families are not isolated — revenue from land settlements paid for the bureaucracy created by administrative acts, while that bureaucracy implemented the educational despatches that trained its own clerks.
Third, the CISCE syllabus expects students to cite specific acts when explaining impacts, so mastering this index turns a vague “British policies” answer into a precise, mark‑fetching response.
Consider the economic family: the Permanent Settlement (1793) fixed land revenue in Bengal, creating a class of zamindars who became political allies.
The Ryotwari system (1820s) in Madras and Bombay dealt directly with cultivators, while the Mahalwari system (1833) in North India used village bodies.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Regulating Act, Pitt’s India Act, Charter Act 1813”) reveals the misconception that constitutional acts are economic policies — confusing administrative framework with revenue extraction.
remember: Name three British acts that belong to the economic policy category in the colonial 50 refs.
Why did the British introduce the Permanent Settlement in Bengal.

cards.title: The land-revenue systems and the colonial economy…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The land-revenue systems and the colonial economy — the money-station in full is this chapter's deep-dive into HOW extraction worked: the machinery, the rates of flow, and the failure-points. (1) THE THREE SETTLEMENTS: the PERMANENT SETTLEMENT (Lord Cornwallis, 1793, Bengal-Bihar-Orissa) — the zamindars recognised as private LANDLORDS of their estates, their revenue-payment to the state FIXED FOREVER, collection rigid (default on the fixed date meant the estate auctioned — the famous "sunset" rule); its chain of effects: the zamindar squeezed the cultivator hard (his own payment was fixed, so every rupee extracted above it was profit), the cultivator's rents rose and his security fell, and the class of zamindar-landlords — often absentee — became the state's rural ally; the RYOTWARI SETTLEMENT (Thomas Munro's system, Madras from the 1820s, extended to Bombay) — the state settling DIRECTLY with each ryot (cultivator), the demand assessed field-by-field on the estimated produce and REVISED periodically; its effects: no middleman, but the state as the hardest landlord — high assessments and rigid collection drove the ryot to the moneylender in bad years; the MAHALWARI SETTLEMENT (from the 1820s, the North-Western Provinces, central India and later Punjab) — the VILLAGE-estate (the mahal) jointly responsible for the land's revenue, assessed on the village and revised periodically; its effects: collective responsibility meant the whole village answered for each defaulter. (2) THE DRAIN IN FULL: India's exports (raw cotton, jute, indigo, grain) earned a surplus abroad; the government used that surplus NOT to buy goods back for India but to meet the HOME CHARGES in London — interest on India's public debt, the salaries and pensions of British officials, the India Office's establishment costs, army expenses charged to India (including imperial wars fought outside India), and purchases of stores — so wealth earned by Indian exports left India without any return flow; DADABHAI NAOROJI named and measured this "drain of wealth" from the 1860s onward (the landmark: "Poverty and Un-British Rule in India", 1901), and RAMESH CHANDRA DUTT's "Economic History of India" (1901–03) documented it historically. (3) THE TRADE'S ONE-WAY SHAPE: India exported RAW materials and imported MANUFACTURES — Indian handicrafts faced duties abroad while British mill-cloth entered India at nominal duty; the looms fell silent and the artisans went to the land (the pressure on land that made every revenue-demand heavier). (4) THE RAILWAYS' FINANCE: built on the GUARANTEE-SYSTEM — British companies raised the capital, and the GOVERNMENT OF INDIA guaranteed them a return (about five per cent in the early contracts), paid from Indian revenues whether the line paid or not; the lines ran where export-traffic wanted them. (5) THE FAMINE-MACHINE: commercialisation had replaced food-grains with cash-crops and the revenue-calendar ignored the rains — so the monsoon-failures of the 1870s became the GREAT FAMINE of 1876–78 (Madras, the Deccan and neighbouring regions; millions dead while grain exports continued); the FAMINE COMMISSION of 1880 answered with famine-codes, relief-works and a famine-fund — the state regulating its own failures. THE STATION'S ONE SENTENCE: the settlements made the state's income CERTAIN while the cultivator's income stayed at the mercy of the rains — and every other element of the economy (the drain, the one-way trade, the guarantee, the famine) hangs on that asymmetry.
steps: The takeaway first: the colonial economy ran on one engineered asymmetry — the state made its own income certain and left the cultivator's at the mercy of the rains — and the three settlements, the drain, the one-way…

The RYOTWARI (Munro, Madras from the 1820s; then Bombay) made certainty DIRECT: no middleman — the state settled with each ryot, field-by-field assessment, demand revised periodically; the theory was tidy, the practice…

The MAHALWARI (from the 1820s; the North-Western Provinces, central India, later Punjab) made certainty COLLECTIVE: the village-estate jointly answered for the whole mahal's revenue, revised periodically — one man's…
Three systems, one design-principle: the government's calendar outranked the monsoon's.

cards.title: British administrative policies (1858–1900) replaced the East India Company’s…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: British administrative policies (1858–1900) replaced the East India Company’s ad‑hoc rule with a uniform, centralized bureaucracy answerable to Parliament. The key pillars were: (1) District Administration – each district headed by a Collector‑Magistrate who combined revenue collection, law‑and‑order, and judicial duties; (2) Indian Civil Service (ICS) – a merit‑based, predominantly British elite cadre recruited through competitive exams in London, forming the “steel frame” of empire; (3) Legal Codification – the Indian Penal Code (1860), Code of Criminal Procedure (1861), and later the Civil Procedure Code imposed a single legal framework across provinces, replacing diverse customary laws; (4) Police Act (1861) – created a disciplined, armed constabulary under the District Superintendent of Police, designed to prevent rebellion rather than serve communities; (5) Limited Indian Entry – from the 1860s Indians could enter subordinate services (deputy collectors, magistrates, police inspectors) and, after 1863, the ICS itself (though barriers remained high). These policies interlock: revenue demands (node 005) required an efficient collectorate; legal codes gave the state coercive power; the police enforced both. The administrative structure also shaped educational policy (node 007) because the government needed English‑knowing Indians for clerical and lower judicial posts. The net effect was a highly centralized, authoritarian governance model that extracted resources, suppressed dissent, yet inadvertently created a western‑educated Indian middle class that later led the nationalist movement.
steps: The British built a highly centralized, district‑based administrative machinery that prioritized revenue extraction and law enforcement over Indian welfare, creating a legacy of bureaucratic control that still shapes…
Here is why: 1.
District Collector as linchpin – After 1858 the Crown made the Collector‑Magistrate the single authority in each district, merging revenue, police, and judicial powers.
This mirrored the Company’s earlier “collector” role but added magisterial duties, ensuring swift revenue collection and immediate suppression of unrest. 2.
Indian Civil Service as steel frame – The ICS, recruited via open competition in London (age limit 21, classical curriculum), became the elite governing corps.
Its members were almost exclusively British until the 1920s; they held all key posts from district to secretariat, guaranteeing policy continuity. 3.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “The Collector only collected land revenue”) reveals the misconception that revenue, police, and judicial roles were separated — they were deliberately fused to strengthen colonial authority.
