Gandhi’s “Do or Die” slogan turned the resolution into a nationwide uprising: strikes, processions, sabotage of railways and telegraph lines, and parallel governments in places like Ballia, Satara, and Tamluk. The British responded with overwhelming force — over 60,000 arrests, including Gandhi, Nehru, Patel, and Azad; press censorship; and military repression that killed hundreds. Though the movement was crushed within months, it demonstrated that British authority rested on Indian cooperation, shattered the myth of “loyal” Indian support for the war, and forced the post‑war Labour government to recognise that independence could no longer be delayed. The movement also linked directly to the subsequent negotiations (Cabinet Mission, Mountbatten Plan) that culminated in the 1947 transfer of power.
steps: The Quit India Movement of 1942 was the decisive mass uprising that forced the British to confront the impossibility of holding India during World War II. Here is why: first, the Cripps Mission’s offer of post‑war…
Second, the British unilateral declaration of India as a belligerent in WWII without Indian consent inflamed nationalist sentiment.
Third, Gandhi’s “Do or Die” slogan transformed a political resolution into a people’s movement, drawing students, peasants, workers, and even some princely‑state subjects into open defiance.

Fourth, the British response — mass arrests of the entire Congress Working Committee, censorship, and military firing on crowds — exposed the moral bankruptcy of colonial rule and galvanised international sympathy.
Fifth, the emergence of parallel governments in Ballia, Satara, and Tamluk showed that Indians could administer themselves, foreshadowing the transfer of power.

Consider the scene in Bombay on 9 August 1942: after Gandhi’s arrest at dawn, thousands of students from Elphinstone College and workers from the textile mills poured onto the streets, shouting “British Quit India!”…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Jawaharlal Nehru gave the call”) reveals the misconception that the most visible political leader always delivers the iconic slogan, confusing Nehru’s later role as prime minister with Gandhi’s moral leadership in 1942.
remember: Who gave the “Do or Die” call during the Quit India Movement.
Why did the failure of the Cripps Mission lead directly to the Quit India Movement.
Assess whether the Quit India Movement achieved its immediate goal of forcing the British to leave India in 1942.

cards.title: The “to Independence” phase (1945‑1947) is the concluding segment of India’s…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The “to Independence” phase (1945‑1947) is the concluding segment of India’s freedom struggle where nationalist pressure, British wartime exhaustion, and international opinion forced a negotiated transfer of power. Key sub‑concepts include: the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946) proposing a united India with grouped provinces; the Interim Government (Sept 1946) led by Jawaharlal Nehru; the Mountbatten Plan (June 1947) accepting partition based on religious majorities; the Indian Independence Act (July 1947) legislating dominion status for India and Pakistan; and the actual transfer of power on 15 August 1947. These events are linked causally: the failure of the Cabinet Mission to satisfy the Muslim League led to the League’s “Direct Action Day” (Aug 1946), which made partition appear inevitable, prompting the British to appoint Lord Mountbatten to oversee a swift exit. The phase also reflects the culmination of nationalism — mass mobilisation (Quit India, INA trials, naval mutiny) created a political climate where British rule became untenable. Relationships: the Quit India Movement (node 007) demonstrated mass resolve; the Cabinet Mission attempted a constitutional solution; its breakdown triggered the Mountbatten Plan; the Independence Act formalised the outcome. Together they show how negotiated settlement, popular pressure, and imperial pragmatism produced independence and partition simultaneously.
steps: The transfer of power in 1947 resulted from a convergence of unstoppable nationalist mass movements and a British government that could no longer sustain its empire after World War II. Here is why: first, the Quit India…

Second, the Cabinet Mission (March‑May 1946) offered a federal scheme to keep India united, but the Muslim League’s demand for a separate Pakistan and the Congress’s insistence on a strong centre made agreement…
Third, the Interim Government formed in September 1946 under Nehru could not function amid League boycott and escalating riots, convincing the British that a quick, orderly exit was essential.
Fourth, Prime Minister Clement Attlee announced in February 1947 that Britain would leave by June 1948;

Lord Mountbatten arrived as Viceroy and, after consulting leaders, advanced the date to 15 August 1947 and proposed the Mountbatten Plan — partition on religious lines with dominion status for both new states.
Fifth, the Indian Independence Act (18 July 1947) passed by the British Parliament gave legal effect to the plan, creating the dominions of India and Pakistan.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “The Plan proposed immediate partition”) reveals the misconception that the Mission’s goal was division, whereas its explicit purpose was unity; the failure to achieve consensus later led to partition.
remember: What was the primary objective of the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946.
Why did the Muslim League reject the Cabinet Mission Plan after initially accepting it.
Evaluate the statement: “The Mountbatten Plan was imposed on Indian leaders without their consent.”.

cards.title: The freedom‑movement registry is a conceptual framework used in the ICSE…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The freedom‑movement registry is a conceptual framework used in the ICSE Class 8 History & Civics curriculum to organise the major phases of India’s nationalist struggle into discrete, comparable nodes. Each node represents a distinct movement or constitutional phase — INC sessions, Moderates vs. Assertives, Partition of Bengal, Swadeshi/Boycott, Non‑Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, Quit India, and the final transfer of power — and captures a standard set of attributes: chronological span, key leaders, dominant ideology, principal strategy (petition, boycott, mass civil disobedience, etc.), immediate outcome, and long‑term significance. By fixing these attributes across all nodes, the registry makes explicit the cause‑effect links (e.g., Partition of Bengal → Swadeshi), the strategic evolution (constitutional agitation → non‑violent non‑cooperation → mass civil disobedience → direct action), and the thematic continuities (nationalist unity, British response, internal debates). It does not replace the detailed narratives in sibling nodes (‑008) but serves as a meta‑tool that lets students navigate, compare, and synthesise those narratives systematically.
steps: The freedom‑movement registry is a structured index that lets students see the entire nationalist struggle as a connected sequence of distinct, dated movements rather than a blur of events.
Here is why: first, it breaks the struggle into eight nodes, each with identical fields — period, leadership, ideology, strategy, outcome, significance — so comparison becomes systematic.

Second, it makes cause‑effect links visible; for example, the Partition of Bengal node (1905) directly feeds the Swadeshi/Boycott node (1905‑1908), showing how a British administrative act sparked an economic‑cultural…

Third, it highlights strategic evolution: the INC Sessions node records early constitutional petitions; the Moderates/Assertives node captures the ideological split; the Gandhian nodes (Swadeshi, Non‑Cooperation, Civil…
Consider a playlist analogy: each movement is a song with genre (strategy), artist (leadership), length (period), and impact (outcome).
The registry is the playlist metadata that lets you sort by year, genre, or artist.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., listing “Home Rule Movement” or “Cabinet Mission” as separate nodes) reveals the misconception that every notable event gets its own node, whereas the registry groups related events under broader thematic movements.
remember: Name the eight movement nodes that constitute the freedom‑movement registry for ICSE Class 8 Chapter 8.
Why does the registry place the Partition of Bengal (1905) before the Swadeshi/Boycott movement.
Assess whether separating Moderates and Assertives into distinct registry nodes accurately reflects the ideological continuity within the Indian National Congress.

cards.title: The Lok Sabha (House of the People) is the lower house of India’s Union…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The Lok Sabha (House of the People) is the lower house of India’s Union Legislature. It consists of a maximum of 552 members: 530 elected from states, 20 from Union Territories, and up to two nominated by the President from the Anglo‑Indian community (currently not exercised). Members are directly elected by universal adult suffrage for a five‑year term unless dissolved earlier. The House is presided over by the Speaker, elected from among its members, assisted by a Deputy Speaker. Its core functions are legislative (passing ordinary and Money Bills), financial (approving the annual budget, scrutinising expenditure), and oversight (question hour, zero hour, motions of no‑confidence). A quorum of one‑tenth of the total membership (55) is required to conduct business. The Lok Sabha enjoys exclusive power over Money Bills — they can originate only here, and the Rajya Sabha can only recommend amendments. The Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha; a loss of majority triggers resignation or fresh elections. The House meets in three regular sessions each year (Budget, Monsoon, Winter) and can be summoned for special sessions by the President on the advice of the Cabinet.
steps: The Lok Sabha is the directly elected house that holds the real legislative and financial power in India’s parliamentary system.
Here is why: it alone can introduce and pass Money Bills, control the national purse, and dismiss the government through a no‑confidence motion.
Consider a classroom where the student council (Lok Sabha) decides the school budget, makes rules, and can ask the principal (Prime Minister) to explain decisions.
First, 543 MPs are chosen every five years by voters in each constituency; any Indian citizen aged 25 or above can contest.
Second, the Speaker, elected by MPs, runs the proceedings, decides on points of order, and certifies Money Bills.
Third, the House meets in three sessions — Budget (February‑May), Monsoon (July‑September), Winter (November‑December) — and needs at least 55 members present to transact business.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “545”) reveals the misconception that the current elected strength (543) is the constitutional maximum, ignoring the nominated seats and the provision for Union Territories.
remember: What is the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha as provided by the Constitution.
Why can a Money Bill be introduced only in the Lok Sabha and not in the Rajya Sabha.
Evaluate the statement: “The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is a member of the ruling party and therefore cannot be impartial.”.

cards.title: The Rajya Sabha, or Council of States, is the upper house of India’s Parliament.
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The Rajya Sabha, or Council of States, is the upper house of India’s Parliament. It consists of a maximum of 250 members: 238 elected by the legislative assemblies of states and union territories through proportional representation by single transferable vote, and 12 nominated by the President for expertise in literature, science, art, and social service. Unlike the Lok Sabha, the Rajya Sabha is a permanent body — it is not subject to dissolution; one‑third of its members retire every two years, ensuring continuity. Its term is six years per member. The Rajya Sabha shares legislative powers with the Lok Sabha except in money matters: a Money Bill can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha may only recommend amendments within 14 days, after which the bill is deemed passed. The Rajya Sabha holds special federal powers under Articles 249 (legislate on State List subjects in national interest), 312 (create All India Services), and 67 (approve proclamation of Emergency). It also participates in the election of the President and Vice‑President and in the impeachment of the President. By representing states as units, it provides a federal check on central legislation and ensures that regional interests are heard in national law‑making.
steps: The Rajya Sabha is the permanent upper house of Parliament that represents the states and union territories, providing continuity and a federal check on legislation.
Here is why: first, its members are chosen by state legislative assemblies, not directly by voters, so each state’s voice is weighted by population but mediated through its own legislature.
Second, the house never dissolves; one‑third retire every two years, which means experienced members remain even when the Lok Sabha is dissolved for elections.

Third, on ordinary bills the Rajya Sabha has equal power — it can amend, reject, or delay — but on Money Bills it can only hold the bill for 14 days and suggest changes, after which the Lok Sabha’s decision prevails.

Fourth, the Constitution gives the Rajya Sabha exclusive powers: under Article 249 it can authorize Parliament to legislate on a State List subject if a two‑thirds majority agrees it is in the national interest; under…
Fifth, the 12 nominated members bring specialised knowledge into debates, enriching legislative quality.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “250 elected members only”) reveals the misconception that nominated members do not count toward the total strength, confusing the separate categories of membership.
remember: What is the maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha and how is it composed.
Why is the Rajya Sabha described as a permanent body.
Assess the practical impact of the Rajya Sabha’s power to delay a Money Bill for 14 days.

cards.title: The President is the constitutional head of the Union Executive…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The President is the constitutional head of the Union Executive, embodying the unity and sovereignty of the Republic of India. Elected by an electoral college consisting of elected members of both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) and the Legislative Assemblies of all states and Union Territories (Delhi and Puducherry), the President holds office for five years and is eligible for re‑election. Qualifications: citizen of India, aged 35 or above, qualified for Lok Sabha membership, and not holding any office of profit under the Union or state governments. Powers are exercised on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister, except in discretionary situations such as appointing the Prime Minister when no party has a clear majority, returning a non‑money bill for reconsideration, or exercising pocket veto. The President also possesses legislative powers (summoning, proroguing, dissolving Lok Sabha; addressing Parliament; promulgating ordinances), executive powers (appointing the Prime Minister, Ministers, Governors, judges of Supreme Court and High Courts, Attorney General, Comptroller and Auditor General), financial powers (causing the Union Budget to be laid, recommending money bills), judicial powers (granting pardons, reprieves, commutations), diplomatic powers (receiving credentials, appointing ambassadors), and military powers (supreme commander of the armed forces). Impeachment requires a charge by either House, investigation by the other, and a two‑thirds majority in both Houses. The President’s role is largely ceremonial, ensuring constitutional continuity and acting as a check on executive excess.
steps: The President of India is the constitutional head who acts on ministerial advice but retains crucial discretionary powers that safeguard the Constitution.

Here is why: the President’s authority flows from the electoral college that represents both the Union and the states, ensuring federal balance; the five‑year term and re‑eligibility provide stability while allowing…

Consider the 1979 scenario when President Neelam Sanjiva Reddy appointed Charan Singh as Prime Minister after the Janata Party split, exercising discretion because no party commanded a clear majority.

Next, the election uses the single transferable vote system of proportional representation, where each elector’s vote value is weighted by state population, ensuring that larger states do not dominate.

Then, the President’s legislative role includes summoning and proroguing sessions, addressing both Houses, and promulgating ordinances when Parliament is not in session — ordinances lapse unless approved within six…
The executive role covers appointments of the Prime Minister, Council of Ministers, Governors, Supreme Court and High Court judges, and key constitutional authorities.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “30 years”) reveals the misconception that the age requirement matches that for Lok Sabha membership (25 years), confusing the higher threshold set for the head of state.
remember: What is the minimum age required for a person to be eligible for election as President of India.
Explain why the President’s election uses an electoral college rather than a direct popular vote.
Evaluate the statement: “The President of India can dismiss the Prime Minister at any time.”.

cards.title: The Vice‑President of India is a constitutional authority established under…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The Vice‑President of India is a constitutional authority established under Article 63 of the Constitution. The office is filled by an indirect election conducted by an electoral college consisting of the elected members of both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, using the system of proportional representation by means of a single transferable vote. The Vice‑President holds office for a term of five years and may be re‑elected. The primary constitutional functions are twofold: first, to act as the ex‑officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, presiding over its sessions, maintaining order, and exercising a casting vote in case of a tie; second, to discharge the functions of the President when the latter is unable to do so due to absence, illness, resignation, removal, or death, until a new President is elected. The Vice‑President does not belong to any political party while in office and must be a citizen of India, at least 35 years old, and qualified for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha. The office is distinct from the Council of Ministers; the Vice‑President is not a member of the Cabinet and does not exercise executive power except when acting as President. The relationship with the President is that of a constitutional successor, while the relationship with Parliament is that of the presiding officer of the Upper House, linking the legislative and executive branches.
steps: The Vice‑President of India is the constitutional deputy to the President and the ex‑officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, elected by an electoral college of both Houses of Parliament.
Here is why: the Constitution creates a separate office to ensure continuity of the executive and to provide a neutral presiding officer for the Upper House.
First, the electoral college consists only of elected members of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha, not state legislatures, reflecting the federal character of the Upper House.
The election uses proportional representation with a single transferable vote, which prevents a simple majority from dominating the outcome and encourages consensus.

Second, as Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, the Vice‑President maintains decorum, decides points of order, and casts a vote only when there is a tie, mirroring the Speaker’s role in the Lok Sabha but without a vote on…

Third, when the President is unable to act — due to death, resignation, removal, or temporary absence — the Vice‑President assumes all presidential powers and duties until a new President is elected or the President…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the people of India directly elect the Vice‑President”) reveals the misconception that the Vice‑President is chosen by popular vote, confusing the office with the President of the United States or a directly elected head of state.
remember: Who elects the Vice‑President of India.
Explain why the Vice‑President does not vote in the Rajya Sabha except to break a tie.
Evaluate the statement: “The Vice‑President can become President for the remainder of the term if the President resigns.”.

cards.title: Ministers are members of the Union Executive appointed by the President on the…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: Ministers are members of the Union Executive appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister under Article 75 of the Constitution. They form the Council of Ministers, headed by the Prime Minister, and are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. The Council comprises Cabinet Ministers (senior ministers heading major ministries), Ministers of State (independent charge or assisting Cabinet Ministers), and Deputy Ministers. Each minister is individually responsible for the administration of his/her ministry and must be a member of either House of Parliament; a non‑member may serve for a maximum of six months. The principle of collective responsibility means that all ministers publicly support Cabinet decisions and resign together if the government loses a confidence vote. Individual responsibility requires a minister to answer for the actions of his/her department. The Prime Minister allocates portfolios, can reshuffle the Council, and advises the President on appointments and dismissals.
steps: The Council of Ministers is the real executive authority in India’s parliamentary system, and it survives only while it enjoys the confidence of the Lok Sabha.
Here is why: the Constitution makes the Council collectively responsible to the directly elected House, so a loss of majority forces the entire ministry to resign.
First, the Prime Minister, as head of the Council, chooses ministers and assigns portfolios, ensuring that each ministry has a political head accountable to Parliament.

Second, ministers are divided into Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State, and Deputy Ministers, reflecting seniority and workload; only Cabinet Ministers attend Cabinet meetings where major policies are decided.
Third, collective responsibility obliges every minister to publicly defend Cabinet decisions, even if they privately disagreed, preventing public dissent that could destabilise the government.
Fourth, individual responsibility makes each minister answerable for his/her department’s actions, allowing Parliament to question specific policies through questions, debates, and committees.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Only the Prime Minister is responsible to the Lok Sabha”) reveals the misconception that responsibility rests solely on the head of government, ignoring the constitutional rule that the entire Council stands or falls as a unit.
remember: What is the collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers.
Why must the Prime Minister be a member of either House of Parliament.
Evaluate the statement: “A Minister can remain in office without being a member of Parliament for up to six months.”.

cards.title: The judiciary is the third organ of the Indian government…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The judiciary is the third organ of the Indian government, entrusted with interpreting and applying the law. It consists of a hierarchical court system: the Supreme Court of India at the apex, High Courts for each state or group of states, and a network of subordinate courts (district, sessions, magistrate, and specialised tribunals). The Constitution guarantees judicial independence through security of tenure, fixed service conditions, and a removal process requiring a two‑thirds parliamentary majority. The judiciary exercises judicial review — the power to examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive orders — and safeguards fundamental rights through writ jurisdiction (Article 32 for the Supreme Court, Article 226 for High Courts). It also resolves disputes between the Union and states, among states, and between citizens and the state. While the legislature makes laws and the executive implements them, the judiciary ensures both act within constitutional limits, thereby maintaining the rule of law and protecting minority rights.
steps: The judiciary is the guardian of the Constitution, ensuring that neither Parliament nor the Executive exceeds its constitutional authority.
Here is why: the Constitution distributes power among three organs, but only the judiciary can authoritatively interpret that distribution.
First, the Supreme Court sits at the top, hearing appeals from High Courts and exercising original jurisdiction in disputes between the Union and states.
Second, each High Court supervises the subordinate judiciary within its territory and issues writs to protect fundamental rights.
Third, district and sessions courts handle the bulk of civil and criminal cases, applying statutes and precedents.
Fourth, judicial independence is secured by fixed salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund, a rigorous impeachment process, and a retirement age that prevents arbitrary removal.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the High Court”) reveals the misconception that state‑level courts outrank the national apex court, confusing the federal hierarchy.
remember: What is the highest judicial body in India.
Why does the Constitution provide a difficult impeachment process for removing a Supreme Court judge.
Evaluate the statement: “Judicial review allows the judiciary to make new laws.”.

cards.title: This node completes the judiciary
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: This node completes the judiciary (node 6 covered the court system's structure — the single integrated hierarchy of the Supreme Court, the High Courts and the subordinate courts); its subject is the judiciary's powers and independence. The Supreme Court's jurisdictions, exactly: original jurisdiction (cases heard first in the Supreme Court itself, exclusively — disputes between the Union and a state, or between states, under Article 131; and the enforcement of Fundamental Rights, Article 32, where the Court issues the writs); appellate jurisdiction (hearings on appeal from the High Courts — constitutional, civil and criminal appeals, for which the Supreme Court is the final court); advisory jurisdiction (Article 143 — the President may refer a question of law or public importance to the Court for its opinion, which the Court may give; the opinion is not binding as a judgment); and its status as a court of record (Article 129 — its records have evidentiary value and it can punish for contempt of itself). The five writs, exactly: habeas corpus ("you may have the body" — ordering the authority detaining a person to produce the detainee before the court and justify the detention), mandamus ("we command" — ordering an authority to perform its public duty), prohibition (stopping a lower court from exceeding its jurisdiction), certiorari (quashing or transferring an order or proceedings of a lower court or tribunal that exceeded its jurisdiction), quo warranto ("by what authority" — challenging a person's right to hold a public office). The powers complete with judicial review — the power to test laws and executive actions against the Constitution and strike down what offends it. The independence of the judiciary is secured by exact safeguards: security of tenure (a judge can be removed only by impeachment — on grounds of proven misbehaviour or incapacity, by a special majority of both Houses of Parliament); salaries and allowances charged on the Consolidated Fund of India and not votable in the legislature; the conduct of judges not discussable in Parliament except on an impeachment motion; a retired judge of the Supreme Court debarred from practising in any court in India; the appointments made by the President in consultation with the senior judiciary (the collegium practice); and the power to punish for contempt, which shields the courts' authority from pressure. Access widened: Public Interest Litigation (PIL) — any public-spirited person may move the court for a victim who cannot (relaxed standing), which opened the courts to the poor; and Lok Adalats — "people's courts" for speedy, inexpensive settlement (their awards deemed court decrees), organised under the Legal Services Authorities framework.
steps: The judiciary's power and its independence are one design, not two topics: the courts can bind the mightiest parties only because no hand can bend the judge — and the full-mark answer walks the design in four circuits.
Circuit one — the four jurisdictions of the Supreme Court.

Original: some cases begin and end in the Supreme Court alone — the exclusive original jurisdiction over disputes the Constitution assigns it: between the Union and one or more states, or between two or more states…
Appellate: the Supreme Court is the final court of appeal — constitutional cases, substantial civil questions and serious criminal matters reach it from the High Courts; its word is the last word.

Advisory: the President may refer a question of law or fact of public importance for the Court's opinion (Article 143) — the Court may give it; the opinion guides but is not a judgment binding parties.
Court of record: its proceedings and records have authoritative evidentiary value, and it may punish for its contempt — the power that keeps its own authority dignified.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., calling an appeal from a High Court part of the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction) reveals the original-appellate…
remember: Name the Supreme Court's jurisdictions and attach the exact example that belongs to each.
Define habeas corpus and mandamus, and construct one situation each in which a citizen would ask for them.
Distinguish prohibition from certiorari — two writs that both deal with lower courts exceeding jurisdiction — and state when each applies.

cards.title: Parliament is the supreme legislative authority of the Union of India…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: Parliament is the supreme legislative authority of the Union of India, constituted under Article 79 of the Constitution. It comprises the President and two Houses: the House of the People (Lok Sabha) and the Council of States (Rajya Sabha). Lok Sabha members are directly elected by adult citizens on the basis of universal adult franchise for a five‑year term, unless dissolved earlier. Rajya Sabha members are elected by the legislative assemblies of states and union territories through proportional representation, with one‑third retiring every two years, giving it a permanent character. Parliament’s core functions include law‑making on subjects in the Union and Concurrent Lists, controlling public finances through the budget and money bills, scrutinising the executive via questions, debates, and committees, and amending the Constitution under Article 368. The President summons, prorogues, and can dissolve Lok Sabha; assent to bills is required for them to become law. While Lok Sabha holds primacy in financial matters (money bills originate only there), Rajya Sabha represents federal interests and can delay non‑money legislation. Together, the two Houses embody the principle of bicameralism, balancing popular representation with federal equilibrium, and serve as the principal forum for national deliberation and accountability of the Council of Ministers.
steps: Parliament is the supreme legislative body of India, consisting of the President and two Houses — Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha — that makes laws, controls finances, and holds the executive accountable.
Here is why: first, the President is an integral part of Parliament, giving assent to bills and summoning sessions, which links the executive head to the legislative process.
Second, Lok Sabha, directly elected by citizens, reflects the popular will and enjoys exclusive authority over money bills, ensuring that taxation and spending reflect the people’s mandate.
Third, Rajya Sabha, representing states and union territories, safeguards federal interests and provides continuity, as it is not subject to dissolution.
Fourth, Parliament’s financial control through the annual budget and the passage of appropriation bills makes the government answerable for every rupee spent.
Fifth, mechanisms like Question Hour, Zero Hour, adjournment motions, and parliamentary committees enable continuous scrutiny of ministers and policies.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Prime Minister, Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha”) reveals the misconception that the head of government is a formal part of Parliament, confusing the executive with the legislative organ.
remember: What are the three components of the Union Parliament as per the Constitution.
Why can a money bill be introduced only in Lok Sabha and not in Rajya Sabha.
Evaluate the statement: “Rajya Sabha is a powerless upper house because it cannot reject a money bill.”.

cards.title: The parliamentary system in India is a form of democratic governance where the…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The parliamentary system in India is a form of democratic governance where the executive branch derives its legitimacy from, and is accountable to, the legislature. The President acts as the constitutional head of state, while the Prime Minister, who leads the Council of Ministers, holds real executive authority. Ministers must be members of either house of Parliament (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha) and are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. The government remains in office only as long as it enjoys the confidence of the majority in the Lok Sabha; a vote of no‑confidence can force its resignation. This fusion of powers contrasts with a presidential system where the executive is separately elected. The judiciary remains independent, interpreting the Constitution and reviewing legislative and executive actions. The system ensures continuous legislative oversight through questions, debates, and committees, making the executive responsive to elected representatives.
steps: The parliamentary system means the government is formed by and answerable to the elected legislature.

Here is why: first, the executive (Prime Minister and Council of Ministers) is chosen from the majority party or coalition in the Lok Sabha, so the same people who make laws also run the administration.

Second, collective responsibility binds all ministers to support cabinet decisions; if the Lok Sabha passes a no‑confidence motion, the entire ministry must resign, ensuring the executive remains responsive.

Third, the President’s role is largely ceremonial — appointing the Prime Minister, summoning Parliament, giving assent to bills — but acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers, so real power stays with elected…
Fourth, the judiciary operates independently, checking both legislature and executive through judicial review, but does not interfere in day‑to‑day governance.

Consider a school analogy: the class monitor (Prime Minister) is elected by classmates (MPs) and must report to them; the principal (President) formally approves decisions but follows the monitor’s lead.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the President directly elects the Prime Minister”) reveals the misconception that the head of state chooses the government, confusing ceremonial appointment with political legitimacy.
remember: What is the primary source of legitimacy for the executive in India’s parliamentary system.
Explain how collective responsibility works when a minister disagrees with a cabinet decision.
Evaluate the statement: “The President of India can dismiss the Prime Minister at will.”.

cards.title: The United Nations (UN) is the international organisation of nations…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The United Nations (UN) is the international organisation of nations established on 24 October 1945, when its founding Charter came into force, "to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war" — the words of its own Charter's Preamble. The road to it: the failure of the League of Nations (founded 1920 after the First World War) — which lacked the great powers' membership and enforcement power and could not prevent the aggression (Japan in Manchuria, Italy in Abyssinia/Ethiopia) that led to the Second World War; the wartime preparations — the Atlantic Charter (August 1941, Roosevelt and Churchill), the Declaration by United Nations (1 January 1942, Washington — twenty-six nations against the Axis, the first use of the name "United Nations", suggested by Roosevelt), the Dumbarton Oaks conversations (1944) that drafted the organisation's blueprint, and the Yalta Conference (February 1945) where the Great Powers settled the voting formula; and the San Francisco Conference (25 April – 26 June 1945), where representatives of fifty nations drafted and signed the Charter of the United Nations (signed 26 June 1945; Poland, not present at the opening, signed later as a founding member — 51 founding members). The Charter's aims (Article 1): (1) to maintain international peace and security, and to bring about by peaceful means and in conformity with justice the adjustment or settlement of international disputes; (2) to develop friendly relations among nations based on equal rights and self-determination of peoples; (3) to achieve international cooperation in solving international problems of an economic, social, cultural or humanitarian character, and in promoting human rights and fundamental freedoms for all; (4) to be a centre for harmonising the actions of nations. The Charter's principles (Article 2): sovereign equality of all members; good-faith fulfilment of Charter obligations; settlement of international disputes by peaceful means; refraining from the threat or use of force against any state; assisting the UN in its action and refraining from assisting any state against which the UN is acting; non-intervention in matters essentially within a state's domestic jurisdiction; and non-members acting in accordance with these principles. Membership: open to peace-loving states which accept the Charter's obligations and are able and willing to carry them out — admitted by the General Assembly on the Security Council's recommendation; from 51 founding members to the present 193. UN Day is observed on 24 October; the headquarters are at New York; the six official languages are Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish.
steps: The United Nations was designed in the shadow of two failures — one of the world's peace (two world wars) and one of the world's first peace-club (the League) — and the full-mark answer walks the design in four moves…
Move one — the failure that taught the design.

The League of Nations (1920) was the first great attempt at organised world peace, born of the First World War's wreckage; it failed for reasons the UN's founders studied like engineers studying a collapsed bridge: the…

The lesson written into every UN bolt: a peace organisation must have the great powers inside it, must be able to decide and act (not merely resolve), and must rest on obligations members accept in advance.
Move two — the building chain, dated.

The wartime allies sketched as they fought: the Atlantic Charter (August 1941) — Roosevelt and Churchill's statement of post-war principles, self-determination and freedom from fear among them; the Declaration by United…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "the UN was founded on 26 June 1945 when the Charter was signed") reveals the signed-versus-in-force blur; a charter exists when signed but the organisation exists when it comes into force — 24 October is the establishment date and UN…
remember: When was the UN established, what event does the date mark, and how many founding members were there.
Why did the League of Nations fail, and which of its lessons are written into the UN's design.
State the four aims of the United Nations in exam-ready form, with the key phrase of each.

cards.title: The General Assembly (GA) is the principal deliberative…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The General Assembly (GA) is the principal deliberative, policymaking and representative organ of the United Nations. Established in 1945 under the UN Charter, it comprises all 193 member states, each with one vote regardless of size or power. The GA meets in regular annual sessions from September to December, and can convene special or emergency sessions. Its functions include discussing any question within the scope of the Charter, making recommendations on international peace and security (except when the Security Council is actively dealing with a dispute), approving the UN budget, electing the non‑permanent members of the Security Council, appointing the Secretary‑General on the Security Council’s recommendation, and electing judges of the International Court of Justice. Resolutions adopted by the GA are generally recommendatory and not legally binding, unlike Security Council decisions under Chapter VII. The GA also oversees the work of the UN’s specialised agencies and funds, providing a forum for global dialogue and consensus‑building. Its relationship with other organs is defined by the Charter: it can refer matters to the Security Council, request advisory opinions from the ICJ, and receive reports from the Secretariat. The GA’s universal membership and one‑state‑one‑vote principle make it the most democratic UN body, reflecting the sovereign equality of all members.
steps: The General Assembly is the UN’s main deliberative body where every member state has an equal voice.

Here is why: it embodies the principle of sovereign equality, giving each of the 193 nations one vote; it serves as the primary forum for discussing any issue within the Charter’s scope; it controls the UN budget and…
Consider a school parliament: every class sends a representative, each has one vote, and they debate school rules, approve the budget, and choose the head prefect.
Similarly, the GA meets annually in New York, debates global challenges like climate change or disarmament, passes resolutions urging action, and approves the UN’s financial plan.
In a special session, it can address urgent crises such as a pandemic.
The GA also elects the ten non‑permanent Security Council members for two‑year terms and, on the Security Council’s recommendation, appoints the Secretary‑General.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “only the five permanent members vote”) reveals the misconception that the GA mirrors the Security Council’s weighted voting, confusing the two organs’ distinct decision‑making rules.
remember: How many member states are currently part of the General Assembly, and what is the voting principle applied.
Why are General Assembly resolutions generally not legally binding, whereas Security Council resolutions under Chapter VII are.
Evaluate the statement: “The General Assembly is the most powerful UN organ because it includes all member states.”.

cards.title: The United Nations Security Council (UNSC) is the principal organ charged with…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The United Nations Security Council (UNSC) is the principal organ charged with maintaining international peace and security. Established in 1945 under the UN Charter, it comprises 15 members: five permanent members (P5) — the United States, United Kingdom, France, Russian Federation, and China — each holding veto power over substantive resolutions, and ten non‑permanent members elected by the General Assembly for two‑year terms with equitable geographic distribution. The Council can adopt binding resolutions under Chapter VII, including sanctions, arms embargoes, and authorization of military action. It also establishes and oversees peacekeeping operations, recommends the appointment of the Secretary‑General, and admits new UN members. Decisions on procedural matters require nine affirmative votes; substantive decisions need nine votes including the concurring votes of all P5 members (the veto). The Council meets continuously at UN Headquarters in New York and may convene emergency sessions. Its work is supported by subsidiary bodies such as sanctions committees and the Military Staff Committee.
steps: The Security Council is the UN’s “executive” for peace and security, uniquely empowered to issue binding decisions that all member states must obey.
Here is why: it combines great‑power consensus (the veto) with broad representation (rotating seats) to act swiftly when conflicts threaten the world.

First, the five permanent members reflect the 1945 victors and hold vetoes, meaning any one of them can block a substantive resolution — this prevents action against a P5’s core interests but can also cause paralysis…

Third, under Chapter VII the Council can impose economic sanctions (e.g., arms embargoes on North Korea), deploy peacekeepers (e.g., UNIFIL in Lebanon), or authorize coalitions to use force (e.g., the 1991 Gulf War…
Fourth, procedural matters need only nine votes, allowing routine business to proceed without vetoes.
Fifth, the Council recommends new UN members and the Secretary‑General, linking security with the organization’s growth.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “20 members with 10 permanent”) reveals the misconception that the Council’s size matches the General Assembly’s larger membership or that permanent seats have expanded.
remember: How many members does the Security Council have, and how many of them are permanent.
Why does the veto power of permanent members exist, and what is its effect on substantive resolutions.
Evaluate the statement: “The Security Council can only impose economic sanctions; it cannot authorize military force.”.

cards.title: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is the principal judicial organ of the…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations, established in June 1945 by the UN Charter and began work in April 1946. It is seated at the Peace Palace in The Hague, Netherlands. The Court consists of 15 judges elected to nine‑year terms by the UN General Assembly and the Security Council voting independently; no two judges may be nationals of the same state. The ICJ has two functions: (1) Contentious cases — it settles legal disputes submitted by states that accept its jurisdiction, issuing binding judgments; (2) Advisory opinions — it gives non‑binding legal advice on questions referred by authorised UN organs and specialised agencies. Its statute forms an integral part of the UN Charter. The Court applies international conventions, international custom, general principles of law, judicial decisions, and teachings of the most highly qualified publicists. Judgments are final and without appeal; compliance relies on the political will of states and, if necessary, enforcement action by the Security Council under Chapter VII of the Charter.
steps: The International Court of Justice is the UN’s chief legal body that settles disputes between countries and advises UN organs.
Here is why: it was created together with the UN in 1945 to provide a permanent, impartial forum for international law, replacing the earlier Permanent Court of International Justice.
First, its 15 judges are elected for nine‑year terms by both the General Assembly and the Security Council, ensuring broad geographic representation and independence.
Second, the Court hears contentious cases only when both states consent — for instance, the 2019 Kulbhushan Jadhav case where India brought Pakistan to the ICJ over consular access.
Third, it issues advisory opinions on legal questions from UN bodies, such as the 2004 opinion on the legality of Israel’s separation barrier.
Fourth, the Court applies a hierarchy of sources: treaties, custom, general principles, judicial decisions, and scholarly writings.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “New York, 1948”) reveals the misconception that the ICJ shares the UN headquarters location and founding year with the General Assembly, confusing the principal judicial organ with the political organs.
remember: What is the seat of the International Court of Justice and in which year was it established.
Explain why the ICJ can only hear a contentious case if both disputing states have accepted its jurisdiction.
Evaluate the effectiveness of the ICJ’s advisory opinions in influencing UN policy, citing one example.

cards.title: UNESCO (United Nations Educational…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: UNESCO (United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization) was established on 16 November 1945 as a specialised agency of the United Nations. Its constitution states three overarching aims: (1) to contribute to peace and security by promoting collaboration among nations through education, science and culture; (2) to advance universal respect for justice, the rule of law and human rights; and (3) to foster the free flow of ideas by word and image. UNESCO operates through five major programme sectors — Education, Natural Sciences, Social and Human Sciences, Culture, and Communication and Information — each guided by an intergovernmental General Conference and an Executive Board. The agency’s most visible work is the World Heritage Convention (1972), which identifies, protects and preserves cultural and natural sites of outstanding universal value. UNESCO also sets international standards such as the Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2021) and coordinates global literacy campaigns. As a UN specialised agency, UNESCO reports to the Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) and collaborates with other agencies (e.g., UNICEF on education, WHO on health‑education links) while maintaining its own budget funded by assessed contributions from member states and voluntary donations.
steps: UNESCO is the UN’s “culture‑and‑learning” arm, created in 1945 to turn education, science and culture into tools for peace.
Here is why: the devastation of World War II showed that military alliances alone cannot prevent conflict; shared knowledge and mutual respect for heritage build lasting bridges.
First, UNESCO’s constitution sets three aims — peace through collaboration, respect for human rights, and free flow of ideas — which directly echo the UN Charter’s purposes.
Second, its five programme sectors translate those aims into action: Education drives literacy and teacher training;
Natural Sciences coordinates oceanographic research and climate monitoring;
Social and Human Sciences promote ethics in technology;
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “UNESCO reports to the Security Council”) reveals the misconception that all UN bodies answer to the Security Council, confusing the Security Council’s peace‑keeping mandate with ECOSOC’s developmental oversight.
remember: What year was UNESCO established and under which UN body does it report.
Explain how UNESCO’s World Heritage Convention helps protect a site like the Taj Mahal.
Evaluate whether UNESCO’s focus on culture duplicates the work of national ministries of culture.

cards.title: UNICEF (United Nations Children’s Fund) was created by the UN General Assembly…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: UNICEF (United Nations Children’s Fund) was created by the UN General Assembly on 11 December 1946 as the United Nations International Children’s Emergency Fund to provide emergency food and health care to children in countries devastated by World War II. In 1953 it became a permanent part of the UN system and dropped “International” and “Emergency” from its name while retaining the acronym. Its mandate covers four core pillars: (1) child survival and development – immunisation, nutrition, safe water and sanitation; (2) basic education and gender equality – enrolment, quality learning, early‑childhood care; (3) child protection – preventing violence, exploitation, trafficking, and supporting children in conflict; (4) policy advocacy and partnerships – working with governments, NGOs, and the private sector to embed child rights in national laws. UNICEF operates through country offices guided by the Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) and reports to the UN Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC). It collaborates closely with sister agencies: WHO for health programmes, UNESCO for education, and the UN Secretariat for coordination. Funding comes from voluntary contributions by governments and private donors, not from the UN regular budget.
steps: UNICEF is the UN’s dedicated agency for children, turning the promise of the Convention on the Rights of the Child into concrete programmes worldwide.
Here is why: first, it was born from an emergency need after World War II, so its DNA is rapid, child‑focused relief.
Second, its four pillars — survival, education, protection, advocacy — cover every stage of a child’s life, ensuring a holistic approach rather than isolated projects.
Third, UNICEF’s voluntary‑funding model lets it stay flexible and respond quickly to crises like floods in Kerala or the COVID‑19 pandemic, unlike the fixed UN regular budget.
Fourth, it works hand‑in‑hand with WHO on immunisation drives (e.g., Mission Indradhanush), with UNESCO on early‑learning curricula, and with the UN Secretariat for coordination across the system.

Consider a village in Jharkhand: UNICEF supplies vitamin‑A capsules and oral rehydration salts through the local Anganwadi, trains ASHA workers on safe delivery, helps the panchayat build a child‑friendly school with…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “1953 as United Nations Children’s Fund”) reveals the misconception that the permanent name change marks the founding date, confusing the 1953 conversion with the original establishment.
remember: What year was UNICEF established and under what original name.
Explain why UNICEF’s funding comes from voluntary contributions rather than the UN regular budget.
Compare UNICEF’s role in child health with WHO’s role. Which agency leads immunisation campaigns in India.

cards.title: The World Health Organization (WHO) is a specialized agency of the United…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The World Health Organization (WHO) is a specialized agency of the United Nations established on 7 April 1948, with its headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland. Its constitution defines health as “a state of complete physical, mental and social well‑being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.” WHO’s core functions are: (1) providing leadership on global health matters, (2) shaping the health research agenda, (3) setting norms and standards (e.g., International Classification of Diseases, vaccine pre‑qualification), (4) articulating evidence‑based policy options, (5) delivering technical support to countries, and (6) monitoring health trends through the World Health Statistics report. WHO coordinates international responses to epidemics (e.g., smallpox eradication 1980, polio eradication drive, COVID‑19 pandemic), promotes universal health coverage, and works with other UN agencies such as UNICEF (child health), UNESCO (health education), and the World Bank (health financing). Its governing bodies are the World Health Assembly (all member states), the Executive Board (34 technically qualified members), and the Secretariat headed by the Director‑General. Funding comes from assessed contributions (mandatory dues) and voluntary contributions from governments, foundations, and private donors.
steps: WHO is the UN’s lead agency for international public health, coordinating global efforts to prevent disease, promote health, and respond to emergencies.
Here is why: first, its constitution gives it a universal mandate that transcends national borders, allowing it to set health standards that all 194 member states agree to follow.
Second, the World Health Assembly, meeting annually in Geneva, adopts resolutions such as the International Health Regulations (2005) that legally bind countries to report outbreaks and share data.

Third, WHO’s technical programmes — Expanded Programme on Immunisation (EPI), Global Polio Eradication Initiative, and the COVID‑19 Solidarity Trial — demonstrate how it translates policy into field action, often…

Fourth, during health crises WHO activates the Health Emergencies Programme, deploys Emergency Medical Teams, and coordinates the Strategic Advisory Group of Experts (SAGE) on vaccines, ensuring rapid, evidence‑based…

Fifth, WHO’s normative work — pre‑qualifying medicines, publishing the Essential Medicines List, and framing the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control — shapes national legislation worldwide, including India’s…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “1945, when the UN was founded”) reveals the misconception that all UN specialised agencies were created simultaneously with the UN Charter, ignoring each agency’s own constitutive process.
remember: What is the date on which the World Health Organization officially came into existence.
Explain why WHO’s declaration of a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) is significant for member states.
Evaluate the effectiveness of WHO’s smallpox eradication programme compared with the ongoing polio eradication effort.

cards.title: The United Nations (UN) was established on 24 October 1945 after the Second…
cards.subject: History & Civics
cards.definition: The United Nations (UN) was established on 24 October 1945 after the Second World War to replace the ineffective League of Nations. Its aims, set out in Article 1 of the UN Charter, are fourfold: (1) maintain international peace and security; (2) develop friendly relations among nations based on respect for equal rights and self‑determination; (3) achieve international cooperation in solving economic, social, cultural, and humanitarian problems; and (4) be a centre for harmonising the actions of nations in attaining these common ends. The principles guiding the UN, listed in Article 2, include: sovereign equality of all member states; fulfilment of Charter obligations in good faith; settlement of disputes by peaceful means; refraining from the threat or use of force against territorial integrity or political independence; giving the UN assistance in any action it takes under the Charter; and non‑intervention in matters essentially within domestic jurisdiction. These aims and principles form the constitutional backbone for all UN organs (General Assembly, Security Council, International Court of Justice) and specialised agencies (UNESCO, UNICEF, WHO), which are covered in separate nodes. India, a founding member, has consistently upheld these principles through peacekeeping contributions and advocacy for decolonisation.
steps: The UN’s aims and principles are the rule‑book that every member country agrees to follow when they join the organisation.

Here is why: the Charter’s Article 1 sets the destination — peace, friendly relations, cooperation, and a centre for harmonising actions — while Article 2 provides the traffic rules — sovereign equality, peaceful…
Consider the aftermath of 1945: the world had just seen two catastrophic wars, and leaders wanted a system that prevented another.
They wrote the aims as a shared vision: “maintain international peace and security” means the UN can authorise peacekeeping missions (India has contributed over 200,000 troops since 1950).
“Develop friendly relations” translates into diplomatic forums where India negotiated the 1972 Simla Agreement under UN auspices.
“Achieve international cooperation” appears in joint health campaigns like the WHO’s smallpox eradication, which India supported.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing C) reveals the misconception that “international cooperation” is limited to trade, confusing the broader humanitarian scope with a narrow economic agenda.
remember: Which of the following is NOT one of the four aims of the United Nations as listed in Article 1 of the….
Explain why the principle of “sovereign equality of all members” is essential for the functioning of the General Assembly.
Evaluate the statement: “The UN’s principle of non‑intervention in domestic affairs prevents it from addressing human rights violations inside a country.”.

cards.title: A percentage (symbol %) is a fraction whose denominator is fixed at 100
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A percentage (symbol %) is a fraction whose denominator is fixed at 100; "68%" literally means 68 out of every 100, or the number 68/100, or the decimal 0.68. Because every ratio is standardised to the same base of 100, percentages allow fair comparison between quantities of different total sizes — 45 out of 60 (75%) can be compared directly with 120 out of 200 (60%). Three conversions sit at the heart of all applications: (i) percentage to fraction — divide by 100 (35% = 35/100 = 7/20); (ii) fraction or decimal to percentage — multiply by 100 (0.45 = 45%); (iii) percentage of a quantity — multiply the quantity by the percentage as a fraction (15% of 4800 = 0.15 × 4800 = 720). Building on these, percentage change measures growth or decline relative to the ORIGINAL value: percentage increase or decrease = (change ÷ original value) × 100. A further application is expressing one quantity as a percentage of another (marks scored as a percentage of total marks) and successive percentage changes, where a second change is applied to the result of the first, not to the original quantity. These ideas form the base on which the whole of this chapter's commercial mathematics — profit and loss, discount, tax, and interest — is built.
steps: Percentage change is always computed on the ORIGINAL value, and once you hold on to this single rule, every percentage problem in commercial mathematics becomes routine.
Here is why the rule matters: a "percentage" is a rate per hundred, and the question "per hundred of what?" must always be answered before multiplying anything.
When a shopkeeper in Kanpur raises the price of a school bag from ₹400 to ₹460, the increase is ₹60, and the percentage increase is 60/400 × 100 = 15% — divided by 400, the old price, not 460.
Now work through the three moves you will use constantly.
Move one: find a percentage of a quantity.
To take 15% of 4800, write 15% as 15/100 and multiply: 15/100 × 4800 = 720.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 3/8 = 38% "rounded" carelessly or 72% = 72/100 left unreduced) reveals the misconception that the conversion is finished at the first step — CISCE papers expect decimals computed exactly and fractions reduced to lowest terms.
remember: Write 3/8 as a percentage, and 72% as a fraction in its lowest terms.
Find 24% of 650.
In a class of 40 students, 26 play cricket. What percentage of the class plays cricket.

cards.title: Profit and loss measure the difference between the cost price (CP)…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Profit and loss measure the difference between the cost price (CP) — the total amount spent in acquiring a article, including every expense incurred to make it saleable — and the selling price (SP) — the amount received when it is sold. When SP exceeds CP, the difference SP − CP is profit; when CP exceeds SP, the difference CP − SP is loss. Profit percent and loss percent are ALWAYS expressed as a percentage of the cost price: profit% = (profit ÷ CP) × 100 and loss% = (loss ÷ CP) × 100. These definitions invert cleanly: SP = CP × (100 + profit%)/100 in a gain situation and SP = CP × (100 − loss%)/100 in a loss situation, so CP = SP × 100/(100 + profit%) or CP = SP × 100/(100 − loss%). The concept links back to percentage change on an original value (node), with CP playing the role of the original value, and forward to overhead expenses (node), where costs beyond the purchase price are folded into CP before any profit is computed. A classical result worth remembering: when two articles are sold at the same price, one at x% profit and the other at x% loss, the seller always suffers a net loss of (x/10)² percent of total cost.
steps: Every profit-and-loss answer is controlled by one fixed rule: the percentage of profit or loss is always calculated on the COST price, never on the selling price.

Here is why this rule has teeth: "profit" names the shopkeeper's gain measured against what the goods cost him, so ₹40 earned on a ₹200 purchase (20%) and ₹40 earned on a ₹400 purchase (10%) are very different…
Fix the four-line toolkit.
Line 1: profit = SP − CP (or loss = CP − SP).
Line 2: profit% = profit/CP × 100.
Line 3: to go forward, SP = CP × (100 + profit%)/100.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "profit happens when profit% is positive" without defining the prices) reveals the misconception that profit is a property of a percentage rate rather than a comparison of two concrete money amounts.
remember: Define cost price and selling price, and state the condition under which a seller makes a profit.
A trader buys a cricket bat for ₹1,250 and sells it for ₹1,430. Find his profit percent.
A shopkeeper sells a radio at ₹1,620 and loses 10%. Find the cost price.

cards.title: Overhead expenses (also called overcharges or incidental expenses) are the…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Overhead expenses (also called overcharges or incidental expenses) are the additional expenditures incurred after the purchase of an article and before it is sold — transport and freight, loading and unloading, octroi and entry taxes, storage and godown rent, repairs and reconditioning, installation charges, and labour. The effective (or net) cost price equals the purchase price plus all overheads: net CP = purchase price + overhead expenses. Once the net CP is formed, the profit-and-loss machinery of node applies unchanged: profit = SP − net CP and profit% = (profit ÷ net CP) × 100. The concept matters because a seller who computes profit on the purchase price alone systematically overstates his gain — every rupee spent on transport or repairs must be recovered through the selling price before any true profit exists. Overheads are part of cost, never part of profit; expenses incurred AFTER the sale (such as delivery to a customer's door when the sale is already complete at the shop) are treated differently and are outside this node's scope. This node sits between profit and loss, which fixes the profit formula, and discount, which refines the selling-price side; together they complete the realistic cost-and-price picture used in tax and interest questions later in the chapter.
steps: An overhead expense is any cost incurred to make an article sale-ready, and the first line of every solution must fold it into the cost price BEFORE any profit is computed.

Here is why: profit is the surplus left after the seller has recovered everything he spent, and if transport, repairs or installation are left out of CP, the seller's "profit" quietly contains money he merely recovered…
Build every solution in three moves.

Move one: list the money spent — purchase price plus every overhead — and add them into a single net CP. Move two: apply the node-2 toolkit on this net CP: profit = SP − net CP, profit% = profit/net CP × 100, or forward…
Move three: when working backwards, subtract the overheads last — recover the net CP from SP first, then remove overheads to find the purchase price.
Watch it work in Surat.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., listing "GST collected from the customer" as an overhead) reveals the misconception that all extra money movements are costs; money charged to the buyer on the selling side is a tax on the sale, not an expense of acquiring the goods, and…
remember: List any four expenses that count as overhead expenses for a trader, and state the formula for net cost price.
A trader buys a sewing machine for ₹9,000 and spends ₹600 on transport and ₹400 on a new belt. He sells it for ₹11,000. Find his profit percent.
A merchant wants a 20% profit on a freezer he bought for ₹18,000, after spending ₹1,500 on delivery and ₹500 on a stabilizer. At what price must he sell it.

cards.title: Discount is a reduction allowed on the Marked Price (MP) of an article…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Discount is a reduction allowed on the Marked Price (MP) of an article, expressed either as an absolute amount (₹) or as a percentage of the marked price. If D denotes the discount amount and d% the discount percent, then - Discount amount D = MP – SP (where SP is the Selling Price). - Discount percent d% = (D / MP) × 100. The relationship links three quantities: Marked Price (the price printed on the tag), Discount (the concession given by the seller), and Selling Price (the actual amount the buyer pays). Discount is always calculated on the Marked Price, never on the Cost Price or Selling Price. It is a key concept in commercial arithmetic, used together with profit, loss, overhead expenses, and tax to determine final transaction values.
steps: Discount is always calculated on the Marked Price, and the Selling Price equals Marked Price minus Discount.
Here is why: the marked price is the reference price set by the seller; any concession is a fraction of that reference.
Consider a shirt marked ₹800.
If the shop offers a 15 % discount, the discount amount is 15 % of ₹800 = ₹120.
The selling price becomes ₹800 – ₹120 = ₹680.
If instead the discount is given as a flat ₹200, the discount percent is (₹200/₹800)×100 = 25 %.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., ₹120) reveals the misconception that discount percent is subtracted from 100 % and then applied to SP instead of MP.
remember: What is the discount amount when an article marked ₹1,200 is sold for ₹1,020.
A pair of shoes is marked ₹2,500. The shopkeeper allows a discount of 12 %. Find the selling price.
Evaluate: “If the discount percent is 20 %, the selling price is 80 % of the cost price.”.

cards.title: A tax is a compulsory charge levied by the government on the sale of goods and…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A tax is a compulsory charge levied by the government on the sale of goods and services; at the Class 8 level the two forms met in problems are sales tax and the Goods and Services Tax (GST), and both are computed as a percentage of the selling price — the price the customer actually pays after any discount. The bill amount equals taxable value plus tax: bill = SP + (tax rate/100) × SP = SP × (1 + rate/100). GST is charged at the point of sale and may be stated as a single rate or split into CGST and SGST, each being half the total rate in intra-state sales (a 12% GST means 6% CGST + 6% SGST). Two placement rules govern every problem: first, tax is charged on the DISCOUNTED selling price, never on the marked price, so a discount is always applied before tax; second, tax belongs to the selling side of the transaction — the seller merely collects it from the buyer and remits it, so unlike the overhead expenses of node it never enters the cost price and never affects the seller's profit. Reverse problems recover the taxable value from a tax-inclusive bill by dividing by (1 + rate/100). This node completes the commercial chain of the chapter: cost (nodes and), price after discount, and finally the statutory addition that fixes the customer's total outlay, before the chapter turns to interest.
steps: Tax is a selling-side percentage: it is charged on the price the customer actually pays, and it passes through the seller to the government without touching his profit.

Here is why placement matters so much: since tax is computed on SP, any discount must be applied FIRST — a Mumbai electronics bill of ₹14,160 on a washing machine whose price is ₹12,000 with 18% GST arises as 12,000 ×…
Fix the three standard computations.
Computation one, forward: bill = SP × (1 + rate/100).
A hotel meal of ₹2,500 with 5% GST bills 2,500 × 1.05 = ₹2,625.

Computation two, backward: a tax-inclusive bill of ₹47,200 at 18% GST contains taxable value 47,200/1.18 = ₹40,000, because the bill is 118% of the price — dividing by 1.18 peels off the tax exactly; the tax component…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "tax is charged on the marked price") reveals the misconception that tax attaches to the tag; the tag price only becomes taxable after the discount is deducted, so charging tax on MP overbills the customer and is exactly the error CISCE…
remember: What is sales tax, and on what value is it charged? State the formula for the final bill.
A pair of shoes is priced at ₹1,600 and GST is 12%. Find the amount a customer pays.
A tourist pays ₹5,310 for a handicraft item including 18% GST. Find the price of the item before tax and the tax amount.

cards.title: Simple Interest (SI) is the extra amount paid or earned on a principal sum P at…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Simple Interest (SI) is the extra amount paid or earned on a principal sum P at a fixed annual rate R\% for a time T years, calculated only on the original principal. The formula is SI = (P × R × T)/(100) and the total amount A = P + SI. Compound Interest (CI) is the interest earned on both the principal and the accumulated interest from previous periods. When compounded yearly, the amount after n years is A = P (1 + (R)/(100) )^n and CI = A - P. When compounded half‑yearly, the annual rate is split into two equal half‑yearly rates R/2\% and the number of periods becomes 2n. The amount after n years (or up to 3 half‑yearly steps) is A = P (1 + (R)/(200) )^2n with CI = A - P. The difference between SI and CI for the same P, R, T arises because CI reinvests interest, so CI > SI for any T > 1 (or for half‑yearly compounding even for T = 0.5 year). Up to 3 years yearly or 3 half‑yearly steps, the difference can be computed directly using the two formulas. The relationship between the sub‑concepts is: percentage → simple interest → compound interest (yearly) → compound interest (half‑yearly). Overhead expenses, discount, and tax (covered in earlier nodes) affect the effective principal or rate but do not change the core interest formulas.
steps: The key takeaway: Compound interest grows faster than simple interest because each period’s interest is added to the principal, so the next period earns interest on a larger base.
Here is why: 1.
Simple interest is linear — the interest amount each year is constant (P × R/100).
Plot SI against time and you get a straight line. 2.
Compound interest is exponential — after each period the principal becomes P(1+R/100) (yearly) or P(1+R/200) (half‑yearly).
The growth factor multiplies, so the curve bends upward. 3.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., ₹1,296) reveals the misconception that the student used the compound interest formula P(1+R/100)^T - P instead of the simple interest formula, confusing the two methods.
remember: What is the simple interest on ₹8,000 at 9% per annum for 2 years.
A sum of ₹5,000 is invested at 8% p.a. compounded yearly for 3 years. Find the compound interest.
Evaluate: For the same principal, rate, and time (2 years), which is larger — simple interest or compound interest compounded half‑yearly? Justify.

cards.title: Two quantities x and y are in direct variation if they change in the same ratio…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Two quantities x and y are in direct variation if they change in the same ratio — whenever x is multiplied by a factor, y is multiplied by the same factor — which happens exactly when their ratio stays fixed: x/y = k, or x = ky, written x ∝ y. Cost varies directly with the number of kilograms bought at a fixed price, distance covered varies directly with time at a fixed speed, and the height of a person varies directly with the length of the shadow cast at a fixed hour. Two quantities are in inverse variation if they change in reciprocal ratios — when x is multiplied by a factor, y is divided by the same factor — which happens exactly when their product stays fixed: xy = k. Speed varies inversely with time for a fixed distance (60 km/h for 2 h, 120 km/h for 1 h cover the same 120 km), the number of workers varies inversely with the days needed for a fixed job, and the number of students varies inversely with how long a fixed stock of food lasts. The single diagnostic question is "which quantity is being held constant?" — constant ratio (a price, a speed, a rate) gives direct variation; constant product (a fixed amount of work, distance, or food) gives inverse variation. These patterns formalise the ratio ideas on which this chapter opened and feed the time-and-work problems of the next node, where "rate of work × number of workers" is precisely an inverse-variation product.
steps: Every variation problem is solved by answering one question first: what is being held constant — a rate (giving x/y = k) or a product (giving xy = k)?

Here is why the question decides the method: direct variation preserves the RATIO, so the missing value comes from equal ratios (a/b = c/d, cross-multiplied); inverse variation preserves the PRODUCT, so the missing…
Walk the two rules through Indian-classroom examples.

Direct: 5 kg of Basmati rice costs ₹420, so k = 420/5 = ₹84 per kg; 8 kg must cost 84 × 8 = ₹672 — the ratio method gives 8/5 = x/420, cross-multiplying to the same x. A 6-metre pole casts a 4-metre shadow at 9 a.m.…
Inverse: 12 workers build a bund in 15 days, so the job measures 12 × 15 = 180 worker-days; 20 workers need 180/20 = 9 days — MORE workers, FEWER days, product intact.
A car covers a fixed 240 km at 60 km/h in 4 hours; at 80 km/h it needs 240/80 = 3 hours, since speed × time is pinned to 240.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "direct means both increase" alone) reveals the misconception that the DIRECTION of change defines the type; doubling x while y grows threefold is "both increase" but not direct variation, because the ratio is not preserved.
remember: State the condition for (a) direct variation and (b) inverse variation between x and y, with one everyday example of each.
For each pair decide whether y varies directly or inversely with x, and give the constant: (a) x = 3, 5, 8 with y = 6, 10, 16; (b) x = 4, 6, 10 with y = 15, 10, 6.
On a road map, 3 cm represents 70 km. Two cities are 9.6 cm apart on the map. Find the actual distance.

cards.title: A time-and-work problem treats the whole job as one unit
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A time-and-work problem treats the whole job as one unit (or as an LCM of the given days) and measures every worker by his RATE — the fraction of the job completed per day. If a worker finishes the job in n days, his one-day work is 1/n; if his one-day work is 1/n, he needs n days. When several workers cooperate, their rates ADD: the combined one-day work is the sum of the individual fractions, and the total time is the reciprocal of that sum — for two workers needing m and n days alone, together they take mn/(m+n) days. Negative rates model obstacles: a leak that empties a full tank in h hours works at rate −1/h and SUBTRACTS from the filling rate.
