cards.title: The electroscope is the instrument that detects electric charge and estimates…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The electroscope is the instrument that detects electric charge and estimates its amount, and this node runs the chapter's static-electricity strand through hands-on activities that lead to it. Static electricity is charge at rest on a body — produced chiefly by friction (rubbing), which tears electrons from one material and deposits them on the other: a plastic comb through dry hair gains electrons (negative), the glass rod rubbed with silk loses them (positive) — unlike mains electricity (node's earlier strand), no continuous flow is involved, only a stored imbalance waiting to discharge. The everyday activity set: the rubbed comb lifting paper bits (the charged comb induces opposite charge in the nearby paper faces and attracts them); the balloon rubbed on hair clinging to a wall; two used polythene refill strips repelling each other (both charged alike); a charged refill bending a thin water stream (water molecules are polar). The gold-leaf electroscope: a metal disc (or plate) on top of a metal rod that ends, inside a dry glass flask or box (dryness prevents charge leaking away through moist air), in two very thin gold (or aluminium) leaves hanging side by side. Working: charge applied to the disc travels down the conducting rod and divides between the two leaves; the leaves now carry like charges and repel each other — they diverge, and the divergence's size tracks the amount of charge. Its four uses at this level: (1) detect charge — leaves diverge when a charged body touches or nears the disc; (2) compare charges — wider divergence = more charge; (3) identify the sign of a charge — first charge the electroscope with a known charge (say, positive from a rubbed glass rod by contact), then bring the unknown body near: further divergence means the unknown carries the same (positive) charge; collapse means opposite (negative); (4) test conduction — touch the disc with any material: a charged electroscope's leaves collapse when a conductor touches (charge flows away through it) and stay put for an insulator. The node's activities discipline mirrors the wiring strand's: charge experiments need dry days (humidity leaks charge), clean dry hands, and the habit of charging one body at a time and observing before touching — the electroscope is the strand's "tester", the instrument that turns invisible imbalance into a visible angle.
steps: Static electricity is charge parked on a body — friction parks it, attraction and repulsion betray it, and the electroscope is the gauge that turns the betrayal into an angle you can measure — three moves, each with its…
Move one — park the charge by friction, and know which way. Rubbing is an electron auction: the material that grips electrons more tightly takes them, leaving the other short.
Comb through dry hair: the plastic comb wins electrons (negative), the hair loses them (positive) — which is why comb and hair attract each other right after, hair strands lifting toward the comb.
Glass rod on silk: the glass loses electrons (positive), the silk carries them away (negative).
Polythene refill on wool/flannel: the refill gains (negative).
The law the kit then demonstrates: unlike charges attract (comb lifts paper), like charges repel (two refill strips, charged the same way on the same cloth, push each other apart when brought close).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "the rod's charge attracts the paper because paper is positively charged") reveals the misconception that neutral objects carry net charge waiting to attract; the paper is neutral overall — its attraction is manufactured by the rod's…

cards.title: Rated power (symbol P, unit watt = W) is the electrical power an appliance…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Rated power (symbol P, unit watt = W) is the electrical power an appliance draws when operated at its designed voltage and frequency under normal load. It is a manufacturer’s specification, printed on the name‑plate. The relationship between power, energy and time is E = P × t where E is electrical energy consumed (kilowatt‑hour, kWh), P is rated power expressed in kilowatts (kW), and t is the operating time in hours (h). One kilowatt‑hour equals 3.6 × 10⁶ joules. Household appliances are grouped by typical rated powers: lighting (5–20 W LED), fans (50–100 W), refrigerators (100–250 W), microwave ovens (800–1500 W), air‑conditioners (1000–2500 W). The rated power allows direct calculation of daily, monthly or yearly energy use and cost when multiplied by the local tariff (₹/kWh). It also informs wiring choices: the current drawn I = P/V (with V ≈ 230 V in India) must be within the safe capacity of the circuit and its protective fuse or circuit‑breaker. This node focuses only on identifying, reading and using the rated‑power value; detailed bill calculation, safety devices and wire identification are covered in sibling nodes.
steps: The rated power on an appliance tells you exactly how fast it turns electrical energy into work or heat when it runs normally.

Here is why: the manufacturer tests the device at standard Indian mains voltage (≈ 230 V) and prints the steady‑state power draw; this single number lets you predict energy use without measuring current each time.
First, find the label — usually a metal sticker on the back or bottom — and note the value in watts (W).
Convert to kilowatts by dividing by 1000 (e.g., 1500 W → 1.5 kW).
Next, decide how many hours the appliance runs in a day (e.g., a fan 8 h).
Multiply: 1.5 kW × 8 h = 12 kWh per day. If the tariff is ₹6 per kWh, the daily cost is 12 × 6 = ₹72.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 8 kW) reveals the misconception that energy and power are directly proportional without dividing by time — confusing total energy with rate of consumption.
remember: What is the rated power of an appliance that consumes 2 kWh when operated for 4 hours.
A 1200 W electric kettle runs for 15 minutes. How many kilowatt‑hours of energy does it use.
Two appliances A (800 W) and B (200 W) are used for the same 5 hours daily. Which contributes more to the monthly electricity bill (30 days) and by how much.

cards.title: A household electricity bill quantifies the electrical energy consumed by a…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A household electricity bill quantifies the electrical energy consumed by a residence over a billing period, typically one month. Energy consumption is measured in kilowatt‑hours (kWh), where 1 kWh = 1 kW × 1 h. The bill lists the meter reading at the start and end of the period; the difference gives total units consumed. Each unit is charged at a tariff rate (₹/kWh) which may vary with slab (e.g., first 100 units at ₹3, next 100 at ₹4). Additional components include fixed charges, electricity duty, and taxes. The bill therefore links three concepts: (1) rated power of appliances (W or kW), (2) duration of use (h), and (3) the tariff structure. Understanding the bill enables estimation of running costs, comparison of appliance efficiency, and planning of energy‑saving measures. It also reinforces the distinction between power (rate of energy use) and energy (total amount used), a key idea introduced in the sibling node on household consumption of electric energy (kilowatt hour).
steps: The electricity bill is a practical application of the energy formula E = P × t, where the bill total is the sum of slab‑wise energy charges plus fixed fees.
Here is why: the meter records cumulative energy in kWh; subtracting the previous reading from the current reading yields the units consumed in the billing month.
Those units are then priced according to the utility’s slab rates, which increase with higher consumption.
Consider a home with a 1.5 kW air conditioner run for 6 hours daily.

Daily energy = 1.5 kW × 6 h = 9 kWh. Over 30 days, that is 270 kWh. If the tariff is ₹3 for the first 100 units, ₹4 for the next 100, and ₹5 thereafter, the energy charge = (100 × 3) + (100 × 4) + (70 × 5) = ₹300 + ₹400…
Adding a fixed charge of ₹50 and 5 % electricity duty on energy charge (₹52.5) gives a total of ₹1152.5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 90 kWh) reveals the misconception that power in watts can be multiplied directly by hours without converting to kilowatts, confusing watt‑hours with kilowatt‑hours.
remember: What is the energy consumed in kWh by a 60 W bulb operated for 5 hours daily over a 30‑day month.

cards.title: Fuses and circuit breakers are the excess-current guards of a household circuit…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Fuses and circuit breakers are the excess-current guards of a household circuit — this node's deep dive into the two devices the safety strand introduced alongside earthing. The fuse: a length of thin wire of a special alloy (low melting point, chosen for its rated current) housed either in a completely enclosed ceramic cartridge fuse (a sealed cylinder with metal end-caps, common in plugs and equipment) or in a rewireable kit-kat type fuse (a porcelain base and a removable carrier where a length of fuse wire is clamped between two terminals — the older Indian domestic standard). It is wired in series with the live wire so the entire circuit current passes through it; its working principle is the heating effect of current: at the rated current the wire runs warm-but-stable, and when the current exceeds the rating the wire's temperature passes the alloy's melting point, the wire melts, and the circuit breaks — the fuse is the circuit's deliberate weak link, renewed (cartridge: replaced whole; rewireable: new wire of the correct gauge) after the fault is found and cleared. The circuit breaker (miniature circuit breaker, MCB, in modern distribution boards): a spring-loaded switch whose contacts are held closed against a latch; the current's own effects actuate the trip — qualitatively, an electromagnetic latch that releases when the current's magnetism exceeds the trip setting (fast, for short-circuits) or a thermal element that bends with sustained overload — the contacts snap apart, the circuit opens, and the breaker resets with a toggle after the fault is cleared, no wire consumed. The rating discipline governs both: the guard's rating is chosen just above the circuit's normal working current, computed from the load as I = P/V (total watts over 220 V) — a 6.8 A heater circuit takes an 8 A or 10 A guard, never a 15 A one "for safety", because an oversized guard relocates the weak link from the device to the wiring. The division of grades: fuse cheap and sacrificial (plugs, small appliances); MCB resettable and precise (distribution boards, one per circuit); and both remain blind to the body-leak fault that earthing (the third guardian) handles. This node, following the bill node, completes the household-management strand: you can now compute the load, guard it, and read the failures.
steps: A guard is a device engineered to fail before the wiring does — the fuse does it by melting, the breaker by tripping, and both obey one rating rule: chosen just above the circuit's honest current, never above the…
The fuse, dissected.
Two chassis, one principle.
The cartridge fuse: a thin wire sealed in a ceramic tube between metal caps — enclosed, so the melt cannot splash; replaced whole; the standard in plugs and equipment.

The rewireable kit-kat: a porcelain base holding fixed terminals and a removable carrier where the fuse wire spans two screws — cheap, and renewable by hand, which is also its weakness: the renewal is only as good as…

Placement: series with the live wire, so every ampere passes through it and, blown on the live side, it leaves the circuit dead rather than still-fed — the two reasons the safety strand established and this node uses…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "the cartridge fuse is safer because ceramic cannot conduct") reveals the misconception that the ceramic's insulation is the safety difference; porcelain is an insulator in both types — the decisive difference is the sealed…
remember: Distinguish cartridge and rewireable fuses in construction and renewal, and state the one risk that the rewireable type carries which the cartridge type largely eliminates.
A circuit on 220 V serves: 4 lamps of 40 W, a 100 W TV, and occasionally a 1000 W….

cards.title: A balloon becomes a simple electrostatic device when rubbed with materials such…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A balloon becomes a simple electrostatic device when rubbed with materials such as wool, silk, or synthetic fabric. Friction causes electrons to move from one surface to the other; the balloon typically gains electrons and acquires a net negative charge, while the rubbing material becomes positively charged. This charge imbalance creates an electric field around the balloon. A charged balloon exerts forces on nearby objects: it attracts neutral objects by inducing temporary charge separation (polarisation) and repels other objects carrying the same sign of charge. The phenomenon illustrates three core ideas — charging by friction, induction in neutral bodies, and the principle that like charges repel while unlike charges attract. Balloons are used in Class 8 as low‑cost, safe tools to make these abstract concepts visible. They also serve as a bridge to the electroscope (covered in sibling node) where the presence and sign of charge can be tested more formally. No quantitative laws (e.g., Coulomb’s law) are introduced at this stage; the focus remains on qualitative observation, correct terminology (electron transfer, static charge, induction), and linking everyday experience to scientific explanation.
steps: A balloon becomes electrically charged when rubbed with certain materials because electrons move from one surface to the other, creating static electricity that can attract or repel other objects.
Here is why: first, friction between the balloon and wool pulls loosely bound electrons from the wool onto the balloon, giving the balloon a net negative charge.

Second, a negatively charged balloon brought near neutral paper bits induces a temporary charge separation — the side of each paper piece closer to the balloon becomes slightly positive, so attraction occurs.
Third, if two balloons are both rubbed with wool, each gains excess electrons; when brought close, they repel because like charges push apart.
Fourth, an electroscope can reveal the presence of charge: touching the charged balloon to the electroscope’s metal cap transfers electrons, causing the gold leaves to diverge.
Fifth, everyday Indian examples make this concrete — a balloon rubbed on a child’s hair at a birthday party sticks to the ceiling, and a rubbed balloon can pick up tiny rangoli powder grains.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the balloon becomes positively charged”) reveals the misconception that the material rubbed always loses electrons, ignoring the triboelectric series which determines the direction of electron flow.
remember: What happens to a balloon when it is rubbed with a woollen cloth.
Why does a charged balloon attract small pieces of paper even though the paper is neutral.
A student claims that a balloon rubbed on hair always becomes positively charged. Evaluate this claim.
